dervis-irab:101-104.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بَصائِرَ): lessons and clear proofs; plural of بصيرة. Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī said:
في الذاهبين الأولين ... من القرون لنا بصائر
(In those who went before, of the bygone generations, there are lessons for us.)
One says: "He has a perspicacity possessed of baṣīra (ذات بصيرة) and possessed of baṣāʾir (ذات بصائر)", meaning a true one; and "I saw upon you the signs of insight (ذات البصائر)". Al-Kumayt said:
ورأوا عليك ومنك في المهد النهى ذات البصائر
(They saw upon you and from you, while still in the cradle, intelligence possessed of insight.)
(مَثْبُوراً): perishing, or turned away from good. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Allah thabara (ثبر) the unbeliever thubūran, of the pattern qaʿada, i.e. He destroyed him; and thabara is used both transitively and intransitively."
(لَفِيفاً): it is said to be a maṣdar (verbal noun) of laffa yaliffu lafīfan, like al-nadhīr and al-nakīr, from laffa al-shayʾa yaliffuhu laffan (to wrap something together); al-alaff is one whose thighs are close together, or one with a large belly. It is also said to be a collective noun with no singular from its own root. The meaning is: We shall bring you all together.

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسى تِسْعَ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ): the wāw is resumptive; the lām is the answer to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation (taḥqīq); آتينا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); موسى is the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object); تسع آيات is the second mafʿūl bihi; بينات is a naʿt (adjective) of the number, so it is accusative (manṣūb), or a naʿt of the thing counted, so it is genitive (majrūr). These signs and the disagreement about them have been mentioned before; we summarise them here according to the report of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: they are the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the stone, the sea, and the mountain (al-Ṭūr) which He raised over the Children of Israel. From al-Ḥasan: they are the flood, the years (of drought) and the shortage of fruits, in place of the stone, the sea and the mountain. Other things have been said which have no relation to this book of ours.
(فَسْئَلْ بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ إِذْ جاءَهُمْ فَقالَ لَهُ فِرْعَوْنُ: إِنِّي لَأَظُنُّكَ يا مُوسى مَسْحُوراً): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the fāʾ that implies an omitted condition) if the address is to Muhammad ﷺ. It is also said that the address is to Moses, in which case it is a conjunction coordinating with an omitted saying, i.e. "So We said to him: ask the Children of Israel", i.e. ask Pharaoh [Translator's note: so in the source]. بني إسرائيل is the second mafʿūl bihi [Translator's note: so in the source]. إذ is an adverb of past time, attached to (mutaʿalliq) آتينا on the first view and to the implied saying on the second; the clause جاءهم is the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb. فقال له is conjoined to something implied, i.e. "when he came to them and conveyed the message to them". فقال له فرعون: a verb and its fāʿil, and له is attached to قال. إني: inna and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); أظنك is an imperfect verb with a latent (mustatir) pronoun as fāʿil, its implied form being "anā", and a mafʿūl bihi. يا موسى: يا is the vocative particle and موسى is a single proper name in the vocative (munādā mufrad ʿalam). مسحورا is the second mafʿūl bihi, i.e. you have been bewitched, so your mind has been confused and your speech disordered.
(قالَ لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ ما أَنْزَلَ هؤُلاءِ إِلَّا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ بَصائِرَ): قال is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, i.e. Moses. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath; علمت is a verb and its fāʿil; ما is negative; أنزل is a past verb; هؤلاء is the mafʿūl bihi, i.e. the signs I have brought; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); رب السموات والأرض is the fāʿil; بصائر is a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "He sent them down as clear proofs". We needed this implied construction only because what comes after إلا cannot be governed by what is before it; some allowed it, in which case it is a ḥāl from هؤلاء.
(وَإِنِّي لَأَظُنُّكَ يا فِرْعَوْنُ مَثْبُوراً): the wāw is a conjunction; inna and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām; the clause أظنك is the khabar (predicate) of inna; يا فرعون is a vocative; مثبورا is the second object of أظنك.
(فَأَرادَ أَنْ يَسْتَفِزَّهُمْ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; أراد is a verb with a latent fāʿil, i.e. Pharaoh; أن with what is in its domain is an interpreted maṣdar, the object of أراد; من الأرض is attached to يستفزهم.
(فَأَغْرَقْناهُ وَمَنْ مَعَهُ جَمِيعاً): the fāʾ is a conjunction; أغرقناه is a verb, its fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi. ومن: the wāw is the wāw of accompaniment (wāw al-maʿiyya) and من is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment); it may also be conjoined to the hāʾ — this will be explained in detail in the Benefits section. معه is an adverb of place forming the ṣila (relative clause) of من; جميعا is a ḥāl.
(وَقُلْنا مِنْ بَعْدِهِ لِبَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ): وقلنا is conjoined to what precedes; من بعده is a ḥāl; لبني إسرائيل is attached to قلنا.
(اسْكُنُوا الْأَرْضَ فَإِذا جاءَ وَعْدُ الْآخِرَةِ جِئْنا بِكُمْ لَفِيفاً): the clause اسكنوا is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); الأرض is a mafʿūl bihi by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa) — this has been explained in detail before. فإذا: the fāʾ is a conjunction and إذا is an adverb of future time; جاء وعد الآخرة is a verb and its fāʿil; the clause جئنا has no grammatical position; بكم is attached to جئنا; لفيفا is a ḥāl.

* Benefits:
The cases of the mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment):
The mafʿūl maʿahu has five cases:
1- Conjunction is obligatory, e.g. كل رجل وعمله ("every man and his work"), and اشترك زيد وعمرو ("Zayd and ʿAmr shared"), because sharing can only come about from two.
2- Conjunction is preferable, e.g. جاء زيد وعمرو ("Zayd and ʿAmr came"), because it is the basic form.
3- The mafʿūl maʿahu is obligatory, e.g. ما لك وزيدا ("what is it with you and Zayd?") [Translator's note: printed «مالك وزيدا»], because conjunction is impossible; and مات زيد وطلوع الشمس ("Zayd died at sunrise"), because conjunction entails partnership, which is invalid here.
4- The mafʿūl maʿahu is preferable, e.g. the poet's words:
فكونوا أنتم وبني أبيكم ... مكان الكليتين من الطحال
(So be, you and the sons of your father, as close as the two kidneys are to the spleen.)
and قمت وزيدا ("I stood up along with Zayd"). In the first example, with conjunction the meaning would be "be [that] to them, and let them be [that] to you", which is contrary to what is intended; in the second example it is not good to conjoin to an attached nominative pronoun except after emphasising it with a detached pronoun.
5- Both are impossible, e.g.:
علفتها تبنا وماء باردا ... حتى غدت همالة عيناها
(I fed her straw and cold water, until her eyes began to flow with tears.)
and the words of another:
إذا ما الغانيات برزن يوما ... وزججن الحواجب والعيونا
(When the beautiful women come out one day, having thinned their eyebrows and [darkened] their eyes.)
As for the impossibility of conjunction, it is because there is no partnership: water does not share with straw in "feeding" (ʿalaf), and eyes do not share with eyebrows in tazjīj, since tazjīj of the eyebrows is making them thin and long — one says rajul azajj and imraʾa zajjāʾ when their eyebrows are thin and long. As for the impossibility of the mafʿūl maʿahu, it is because there is no accompaniment in the first verse, since water does not accompany straw in feeding, and because in the second verse there is no benefit in informing that the eyes accompany the eyebrows, as it is known that the eyes accompany the eyebrows, so there is no benefit in informing of it. In such cases one must imply a verb that puts the noun after the wāw in the accusative as a mafʿūl bihi, i.e. "I fed her straw and gave her cold water to drink" (saqaytuhā), and "they thinned the eyebrows and applied kohl to the eyes" (kaḥḥalna).

dervis-irab:105-111.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مُكْثٍ): with the mīm pronounced with any of the three vowels (mukth, makth, mikth), i.e. length of time, at leisure and deliberately; no reading with kasra has come down.
(الْأَذْقانِ): plural of dhaqan (chin), which is where the two jawbones meet. A detailed discussion will come in the Rhetoric section.
(تُخافِتْ): to speak secretly. One says khafata al-ṣawt, on the patterns of ḍaraba and jalasa, when the voice is quiet; it is made transitive with bāʾ, so one says khafata al-rajulu bi-ṣawtihi when he does not raise it, and khāfata bi-qirāʾatihi mukhāfatatan when he does not raise his voice in it; and khafata al-zarʿ and the like means it died, so it is khāfit.

* I'rab:
(وَبِالْحَقِّ أَنْزَلْناهُ وَبِالْحَقِّ نَزَلَ): the speech here is connected to what preceded of the words of Allah the Exalted about the Quran, namely His saying «قل لئن اجتمعت الانس والجن» etc., by way of digression (istiṭrād), as is customary in the styles of the Arabs, who move from the subject they are on to another and then return to it. In any case, the wāw is resumptive; بالحق is attached to (mutaʿalliq) أنزلناه; أنزلناه is a verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); بالحق is attached to نزل. The bāʾ is causal in both; you may also make it for accompaniment (mulābasa), in which case the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "bound up with (the truth)", and the ḥāl is from the mafʿūl bihi; or "We being bound up with the truth", in which case the ḥāl is from the fāʿil. More of this discussion will come in the Rhetoric section.
(وَما أَرْسَلْناكَ إِلَّا مُبَشِّراً وَنَذِيراً): the wāw is a conjunction; ما is negative; أرسلناك is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); مبشرا is a ḥāl and نذيرا is conjoined to it. Discussion of this restriction (qaṣr) will come in the Rhetoric section.
(وَقُرْآناً فَرَقْناهُ لِتَقْرَأَهُ عَلَى النَّاسِ عَلى مُكْثٍ وَنَزَّلْناهُ تَنْزِيلًا): قرآنا is accusative by ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb), governed by an omitted verb explained by what follows, so the clause فرقناه is explicative, i.e. We made its revelation separated and in instalments, according to events, incidents and the requirements of circumstances. لتقرأه: the lām is causal (for taʿlīl), and تقرأه is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن; the preposition and its genitive (the interpreted maṣdar) are attached to فرقناه. فرقناه is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; على الناس is attached to تقرأه; على مكث is in the position of a ḥāl from the fāʿil, i.e. taking your time, unhurried, and bit by bit [Translator's note: printed «شيئا بعد شيئا»], out of regard for the interests and livelihoods of the servants. نزلناه is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; تنزيلا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(قُلْ آمِنُوا بِهِ أَوْ لا تُؤْمِنُوا): the clause آمنوا is the maqūl al-qawl (object of the saying); the imperative is for contempt, i.e. your belief or its absence is the same to Us, for you are not people anyone pays attention to. أو لا تؤمنوا: أو is a conjunction, لا is prohibitive, and تؤمنوا is jussive (majzūm) by لا.
(إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ إِذا يُتْلى عَلَيْهِمْ يَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقانِ سُجَّداً): inna and its noun; the clause أوتوا العلم is the ṣila (relative clause); العلم is the second object of أوتوا, and the first is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent), which is the wāw; من قبله is a ḥāl. The clause gives the reason (taʿlīl) for the saying, by way of consoling him ﷺ. إذا is an adverb of future time attached to يخرون; the clause يتلى is the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb; عليهم is attached to يتلى; the clause يخرون has no grammatical position because it is the answer of إذا; للأذقان is attached to يخرون; سجدا is a ḥāl.
(وَيَقُولُونَ سُبْحانَ رَبِّنا إِنْ كانَ وَعْدُ رَبِّنا لَمَفْعُولًا): ويقولون is conjoined to يخرون; سبحان ربنا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq; إن is lightened (mukhaffafa) and inoperative (muhmala), and its noun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) [Translator's note: so in the source, which calls it both "inoperative" and gives it a noun]; the clause كان is its khabar (predicate); وعد ربنا is the noun of kāna; the lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa); مفعولا is its (kāna's) khabar.
(وَيَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقانِ يَبْكُونَ وَيَزِيدُهُمْ خُشُوعاً): the clause is conjoined to the one before it — the secret of this repetition will come in the Rhetoric section. The clause يبكون is a ḥāl. The wāw is the wāw of circumstance [Translator's note: so in the source, though there is no wāw before يبكون; the wāw of ويزيدهم may be meant]. يزيدهم is a verb with a latent (mustatir) fāʿil, the hāʾ is the first mafʿūl bihi and خشوعا is the second mafʿūl bihi. The secret of these two successive circumstantial clauses will come in the Rhetoric section.
(قُلِ ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوِ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمنَ): they heard Muhammad calling on one occasion in his prostration, saying "O Allah, O Raḥmān", and Abū Jahl said: "Muhammad forbids us our gods while he himself calls on two gods!" So this was revealed. The clause ادعوا الله is the maqūl al-qawl. The duʿāʾ here means naming, not calling; in this sense it takes two objects, one of which has been omitted as unnecessary because it is known. The word of majesty (Allah) is the mafʿūl bihi. أو is for choice (takhyīr), so it is a conjunction; ادعوا is conjoined to the first ادعوا, and الرحمن is a mafʿūl bihi, i.e. name Him by this name or that.
(أَيًّا ما تَدْعُوا فَلَهُ الْأَسْماءُ الْحُسْنى): أيا is conditional; it is accusative by تدعوا as a preposed object. ما is redundant (zāʾida), for emphatic vagueness. تدعوا is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), and the sign of its jussive is the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil. The fāʾ connects the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) because it is a nominal clause; له is a preposed khabar, الأسماء is a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), and الحسنى is a naʿt (adjective). It has also been said that ما is conditional, and the two conditional particles are combined for emphasis and because the two words differ — but there is no need for this. The Beautiful Names will come in the Benefits section.
(وَلا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلاتِكَ وَلا تُخافِتْ بِها وَابْتَغِ بَيْنَ ذلِكَ سَبِيلًا): the wāw is a conjunction, لا is prohibitive, تجهر is an imperfect verb in the jussive by لا, and the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "anta". He was forbidden to speak aloud in order to avoid their insults, and this is among the fine points of good conduct. ولا تخافت is conjoined to ولا تجهر, i.e. do not make it inaudible to those praying behind you. ابتغ is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the weak letter. بين is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was originally a naʿt of سبيلا; ذلك is the muḍāf ilayhi of the adverb. The demonstrative points to two things, namely speaking aloud and speaking quietly, which is why it is correct for بين to be used with it. سبيلا is the object of ابتغ.
(وَقُلِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَّخِذْ وَلَداً): the clause الحمد لله is the maqūl al-qawl; الحمد is the mubtadaʾ and لله the khabar; الذي is a naʿt; the clause لم يتخذ ولدا is the ṣila. Praise is made to follow from His not taking a son because whoever is described thus is, without doubt, the One able to lavish blessings and bestow them; whereas one who has a son is exposed to being distracted by his son from others and occupied with his children rather than anyone else.
(وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ شَرِيكٌ فِي الْمُلْكِ): conjoined to لم يتخذ. لم is a particle of negation, inversion (of the tense) and jussive; يكن is an incomplete (nāqiṣ) imperfect verb in the jussive by لم; له is its preposed khabar; شريك is its postponed noun; في الملك is attached to شريك. The negation of a partner is a greater cause for praise, because there is no rival whose will would conflict with His.
(وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ وَلِيٌّ مِنَ الذُّلِّ وَكَبِّرْهُ تَكْبِيراً): conjoined to what precedes. The negation of a helper indicates self-sufficiency, and only the strong One who is able to increase His favours is self-sufficient. من الذل is attached to ولي, i.e. a helper. كبّره is conjoined to قل; it is an imperative verb with a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; تكبيرا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq for emphasis.

* Rhetoric:
The closing verses of Sūrat al-Isrāʾ are rich in a number of rhetorical devices, which we summarise as follows. The first of them:
1- Explicit mention (al-dhikr), or explicitness (al-taṣrīḥ):
In the saying of Allah the Exalted «وبالحق أنزلناه وبالحق نزل»: had He abandoned the overt noun and turned to a pronoun, as the context would require, saying "and with the truth We sent it down and with it it came down", it would not have had the grandeur it has now. Some call this taṣrīḥ, and cite as evidence for it the saying of al-Buḥturī:
قد طلبنا فلم نجد لك في السوء ... دد والمجد والمكارم مثلا
(We sought, but found no equal to you in lordship, glory and noble deeds.)
The meaning is: we sought an equal and did not find one. It was omitted (after "sought") because this praise is only complete in "equal", while the seeking is like something mentioned in order to build the intended purpose upon it. That being so, he said: we sought an equal in lordship and glory and did not find one. Of this kind is the saying of Allah the Exalted «قل هو الله أحد الله الصمد»: had He abandoned the overt noun for a pronoun and said "Say: He is Allah, and He is the Eternal Refuge", it would not have had the fitting impact.
2- The device of digression (istiṭrād):
Istiṭrād: al-Ḥātimī mentioned in Qawāʿid al-Shiʿr that he took this name from the poet al-Buḥturī; Ibn al-Muʿtazz called it "going out from one idea to another", and others defined it as the speaker being on one of the topics, giving the impression that he is continuing in it, then leaving it for another because of an affinity between the two, then returning to the first and cutting the speech short. Thus He, glory be to Him, moved from His speech about the Quran — that men and jinn are incapable of producing its like in eloquence and rhetoric even if they backed one another up — moved to the parables, lessons and clear proofs contained in it, and the speech was carried on to the obstinacy of the unbelievers, their persistence in contention, their blind continuance in error and arrogance, their obliterating of truths and denial of facts. Then He brought as evidence of this what Moses met with of the arrogance of Pharaoh and his chiefs, and struck an example in the outcome that befell Pharaoh and those with him; then He returned to the subject He had begun with, namely that the Quran came down with the truth and aims at it.
Among the charming instances of istiṭrād is the famous saying of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib:
لنا نفوس لنيل المجد عاشقة ... فإن تسلّت أسلناها على الأسل
لا ينزل المجد إلا في منازلنا ... كالنوم ليس له مأوى سوى المقل
(We have souls in love with attaining glory; if they turn away, we make them flow on the spear-points. Glory dwells only in our dwellings, like sleep, which has no shelter but the eyes.)
He digressed from mentioning glory to sleep. Poets have exploited it for satire; one of them said, satirising the poetry of Khālid al-Kātib:
وشادن بالدلال عاتبني ... ومنيتي في تدلل العاتب
فكان ردي عليه من خجلي ... أبرد من شعر خالد الكاتب
(A fawn reproached me coquettishly — and my wish lies in the coquetry of the reproacher — so my reply to him, out of my embarrassment, was colder than the poetry of Khālid al-Kātib.)
How beautiful this digression is! He was composing love poetry about the fawn, and there is none colder than one who reproaches the sweet and beautiful one and answers him back when he is coquettish or reproachful; whoever forces himself to such a reply will produce only cold speech resembling the poetry of Khālid al-Kātib. Beautiful too is the saying of one who satirised the chief judge, moving from describing a garden to his real purpose:
لله بستان حللنا دوحه ... في جنة قد فتحت أبوابها
والبان تحسبه سنانيرا رأت ... قاضي القضاة فنفشت أ. ذنابها
(How fine a garden whose great trees we alighted among, in a paradise whose gates were opened; and the ban trees you would think were cats that saw the chief judge and fluffed up their tails.) [Translator's note: the source prints «أ. ذنابها», evidently for «أذنابها».]
Al-Bākharzī cites in Dumyat al-Qaṣr, from al-Ẓāhir al-Ḥaramī, these verses in which he satirises a singer named al-Burqaʿīdī:
وليل كوجه البرقعيدي ظلمة ... وبرد أغانيه وطول قرونه
قطعت دياجيه بنوم مشرّد ... كعقل سليمان بن فهد ودينه
على أولق فيه التفات كأنه ... أبو جابر في خبطه وجنونه
إلى أن بدا ضوء الصباح كأنه ... سنا وجه قرواش وضوء جبينه
(And a night like the face of al-Burqaʿīdī in darkness, in the coldness of his songs and the length of his locks; I traversed its gloom with a sleep that kept fleeing, like the mind and religion of Sulaymān ibn Fahd, in a frenzy full of twisting, as if it were Abū Jābir in his blundering and madness — until the light of morning appeared, like the radiance of Qirwāsh's face and the brightness of his brow.)
3- Restriction (qaṣr) and its methods:
In His saying «وما أرسلناك إلا مبشرا ونذيرا» there is a relative restriction (qaṣr iḍāfī). Qaṣr is the specification of one thing to another by a particular method. It is divided into real and relative. Real restriction is that in which the specification holds according to fact and reality, not relative to something else, e.g. "There is no writer in the city except ʿAlī", if there is no other writer in it. Relative restriction is that in which the specification holds relative to a particular thing, e.g. "ʿAlī is nothing but standing", i.e. he has the quality of standing, not the quality of sitting. Each of them is divided into restriction of a quality to a described thing, e.g. "There is no horseman except ʿAlī", and restriction of a described thing to a quality, e.g. «وما محمد إلا رسول».
Relative restriction is divided, with respect to the state of the addressee, into three types: qaṣr ifrād (restriction of singling out), when the addressee believes in partnership; qaṣr qalb (restriction of reversal), when he believes the opposite; and qaṣr taʿyīn (restriction of specification), when he believes one of two things without specifying it.
Qaṣr has four well-known methods and many less well-known ones. The four well-known ones are:
a- Negation and exception: here the thing restricted to (al-maqṣūr ʿalayhi) is what comes after the particle of exception, e.g. "None succeeds but the diligent": success is the restricted (maqṣūr) and the diligent is the thing restricted to; this is restriction of a quality to a described thing.
b- «إنما», where the thing restricted to must come last. ʿAbd al-Qāhir's discussion of innamā has preceded. E.g. "Life is only toil": life is restricted and toil is the thing restricted to; this is restriction of a described thing to a quality.
c- Conjunction with لا, بل or لكن. If the conjunction is with لا, the thing restricted to is the counterpart of what follows it, e.g. "The earth is moving, not stationary"; if it is with بل or لكن, the thing restricted to is what comes after them, e.g. "The earth is not stationary, but rather moving", and "The earth is not stationary, but moving".
d- [Translator's note: the source labels this item «هـ».] Preposing what ought to come later; here the thing restricted to is what is preposed, e.g. "It is the working men that we praise" (على الرجال العاملين نثني).
There are other methods of qaṣr besides these four, among them the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), e.g. "ʿAlī — he is the brave one", and the explicit use of the word «وحده» as a ḥāl, or «ليس غير», e.g. "I honoured ʿAlī alone"; but these are not counted among its technical methods.
4- Repetition in meaning (al-takrīr al-maʿnawī):
The discussion of verbal repetition has preceded. The repetition we are dealing with here relates to meaning. He repeated the falling to the chins — that is, falling on the face — because the two states differ: the first is their falling while prostrating, and the second their falling while weeping; or the first is when hearing or reciting the Quran and the second in all other states. Then He followed the two states with a third, namely their increasing in humility whenever they recite and whenever they prostrate, thus covering all their states — and they are the perfect ones who were given knowledge. It must be pointed out that He brought the first ḥāl as a noun, namely سجدا, to indicate continuity, and the second ḥāl as a verb, to indicate renewal and occurrence, as if their weeping is renewed with the renewal of the circumstances that befall them and the successive admonitions. This is a difficult place of repetition, the knowledge of which is too subtle for the inexperienced.
Among what has come of it is the ḥadīth of Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa [Translator's note: printed «حاطب بن بلتعة»] in the campaign of the Conquest. The Prophet ﷺ commanded ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Zubayr and al-Miqdād, may Allah be pleased with them, saying: "Go to Rawḍat Khākh, for there is a woman traveller there who has a letter with her; bring it to me." ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We set out, our horses racing with us, until we came to the Rawḍa, and there was the woman; we took the letter from her braids and brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it was from Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa to some of the polytheists in Mecca, informing them of some of the affairs of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said to him: "What is this, O Ḥāṭib?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not be hasty with me. I was a man attached to Quraysh but not one of them, and those of the Emigrants who are with you have kinsmen there by whom they protect their property and families in Mecca. Since I lacked that kinship, I wanted to do them a favour by which they would protect my relatives. I did not do it out of unbelief, nor apostasy from my religion, nor contentment with unbelief after Islam." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He has told you the truth."
His words "I did not do it out of unbelief, nor apostasy from my religion, nor contentment with unbelief after Islam" are a fine repetition which some ignorant people think is repetition without benefit [Translator's note: printed «فبه» for «فيه»], since unbelief and apostasy from religion are the same, and likewise contentment with unbelief after Islam. But it is not so. What the wording indicates is: I did not do that while being an unbeliever, i.e. remaining in unbelief; nor as an apostate, i.e. that I disbelieved after my Islam; nor out of contentment with unbelief after Islam, i.e. nor out of preferring the side of the unbelievers to the side of the Muslims. This is very good and well placed; but these are the requirements of circumstances and ramifications whose recesses only the inquisitive person of refined taste explores.
Among what has come in poetry of this repetition in meaning is the saying of al-Muqannaʿ al-Kindī, which we cite in full because of its importance:
يعاتبني في الدّين قومي وإنما ... ديوني في أشياء تكسبهم حمدا
أسدّ به ما قد أخلوا وضيعوا ... ثغور حقوق ما أطاقوا لها سدا
وإن الذي بيني وبين بني أبي ... وبين بني عمي لمختلف جدا
فإن أكلوا لحمي وفرت لحومهم ... وإن هدموا مجدي بنيت لهم مجدا
وإن ضيعوا غيبي حفظت غيوبهم ... وإن هم هووا عني هويت لهم رشدا
وان زجروا طيرا بنحس تمر بي ... زجرت لهم طيرا تمر بهم سعدا
ولا أحمل الحقد القديم عليهم ... وليس رئيس القوم من يحمل الحقدا
وليسوا إلى نصري سراعا وان هم ... دعوني إلى نصر أتيتهم شدا
وإني لعبد الضيف ما دام ثاويا ... وما شيمة لي غيرها تشبه العبدا
(My people blame me for my debts, but my debts are for things that earn them praise; with them I fill the gaps of obligations they have neglected and lost, which they could not fill. What is between me and my father's sons and my cousins is very different: if they eat my flesh, I spare their flesh; if they demolish my glory, I build glory for them; if they neglect me in my absence, I guard them in theirs; if they wish me ill, I wish them right guidance; if they augur from birds an ill omen passing me, I augur for them birds passing them with good fortune. I bear no old rancour against them — the chief of a people is not one who bears rancour. They are not quick to help me, but if they call me to help, I come to them running. I am the slave of the guest as long as he stays, and I have no trait besides this that resembles a slave.) [Translator's note: the printed text runs the last lines together; they are set out here by verse.]
For every eating of a man's flesh is a neglect of him in his absence, but not every neglect of him in his absence is an eating of his flesh. Do you not see that eating flesh is backbiting, whereas neglecting him in his absence includes backbiting, abandoning support and help, and neglecting to strive for whatever brings benefit, whatever it may be? This is something that occurs in eloquent speech, and the ignorant think there is no benefit in it.

* Benefits:
1- The Beautiful Names:
"Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has ninety-nine names, a hundred less one. He is Odd (witr) and loves what is odd. Whoever enumerates them enters Paradise. They are: He is Allah, besides whom there is no god, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Malik, al-Quddūs, al-Salām, al-Muʾmin, al-Muhaymin, al-ʿAzīz, al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir, al-Khāliq, al-Bāriʾ, al-Muṣawwir, al-Ghaffār, al-Qahhār, al-Wahhāb, al-Razzāq, al-Fattāḥ, al-ʿAlīm, al-Qābiḍ, al-Bāsiṭ, al-Khāfiḍ, al-Rāfiʿ, al-Muʿizz, al-Mudhill, al-Samīʿ, al-Baṣīr, al-Ḥakam, al-ʿAdl, al-Laṭīf, al-Khabīr, al-Ḥalīm, al-ʿAẓīm, al-Ghafūr, al-Shakūr, al-ʿAlī, al-Kabīr, al-Ḥafīẓ, al-Muqīt (i.e. the All-Powerful), al-Ḥasīb, al-Jalīl, al-Karīm, al-Raqīb, al-Mujīb, al-Wāsiʿ, al-Ḥakīm, al-Wadūd, al-Majīd, al-Bāʿith, al-Shahīd, al-Ḥaqq, al-Wakīl, al-Qawī, al-Matīn, al-Walī, al-Ḥamīd, al-Muḥṣī, al-Mubdiʾ, al-Muʿīd, al-Muḥyī, al-Mumīt, al-Ḥayy, al-Qayyūm, al-Wājid, al-Mājid, al-Wāḥid, al-Aḥad, al-Ṣamad, al-Qādir, al-Muqtadir, al-Muqaddim, al-Muʾakhkhir, al-Awwal, al-Ākhir, al-Ẓāhir, al-Bāṭin, al-Wālī, al-Mutaʿālī, al-Barr, al-Tawwāb, al-Muntaqim, al-ʿAfuww, al-Raʾūf, Mālik al-Mulk, Dhū al-Jalāl wa-al-Ikrām, al-Muqsiṭ, al-Jāmiʿ, al-Ghanī, al-Mughnī, al-Māniʿ, al-Ḍārr, al-Nāfiʿ, al-Nūr, al-Hādī, al-Badīʿ, al-Bāqī, al-Wārith, al-Rashīd, al-Ṣabūr."
2- Speaking aloud and quietly, and an explanation of the reason for it:
After Quraysh found that entering into debates with the Prophet would avail them nothing, having been repeatedly defeated before the splendid proofs and divine miracles with which he overwhelmed them [Translator's note: printed «يبدها»], and after they felt they had no power to challenge the Quran and its sacred authority over souls, they settled on resorting to another kind of passive resistance, namely refusing completely to listen to the Quran. Ibn Isḥāq related: whenever the Messenger recited the Quran aloud while praying, they would disperse from him and refuse to listen to him; and if a man among them wanted to hear from the Messenger of Allah some of what he was reciting of the Quran while praying, he would eavesdrop secretly from them out of fear of them; if he saw that they had realised he was listening to him, he would go away fearing their harm and not listen. And if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lowered his voice, and the one listening thought that they were not hearing anything of his recitation while he himself heard something they did not, he would lend his ear to listen to him.
Ibn ʿAbbās related that this verse «ولا تجهر بصلاتك» etc. was revealed only on account of these people.
And although the leaders of Quraysh had called the people of Mecca to turn away from listening to the Quran, they had no power to carry out this command, because of the tenderness they felt in themselves and their eagerness to hear this revelation, the like of which they had never known.
Ibn Isḥāq also related:
Abū Sufyān, Abū Jahl and al-Akhnas went out one night to listen to the Messenger of Allah while he was praying at night in his house. Each of them took a place to listen from, none knowing where his companion was. They spent the night listening until, when dawn broke, they dispersed; the road brought them together, and they blamed one another, and said to one another: "Do not come back, for if one of your fools saw you, you would put something into his mind." Then they left. When it was the second night, each man returned to his place, and they spent the night listening to him until, when dawn broke, they dispersed; the road brought them together, and they said to one another the same as they had said the first time, then left. When it was the third night, each man took his place, and they spent the night listening to him until dawn broke; they dispersed, the road brought them together, and they said to one another: "We will not leave until we pledge not to come back." So they pledged that, then dispersed.
In the morning al-Akhnas took his staff and went out until he came to Abū Sufyān in his house, and said to him:
- Tell me, O Abū Ḥanẓala, your opinion of what you heard from Muhammad. He said:
- O Abū Thaʿlaba, by Allah, I heard things that I know and know what is meant by them, and I heard things whose meaning I did not know nor what was meant by them. Al-Akhnas said to him:
- And I, by Him by whom you swore, am the same.
Then he left him and came to Abū Jahl, entered his house and said to him:
- O Abū al-Ḥakam, what is your opinion of what you heard from Muhammad? He said:
- What did I hear? We and Banū ʿAbd Manāf contended for honour: they fed, so we fed; they gave, so we gave; until, when we were knee to knee and were like two racehorses, they said: "Among us is a prophet to whom revelation comes from heaven." When will we ever attain the like of this? By Allah, we will never believe in him nor accept him as truthful. So al-Akhnas rose and left him.
Thus Quraysh were bewildered in their affair: their hearts softened and their souls were humbled before the Quran, because they perceived its secrets, penetrated its eloquence and plumbed its depths; yet tribal partisanship, the insignia of leadership and the conditions of the Jāhiliyya — all of this kept them from Islam. More of this charming and lofty discussion will come ...

dervis-irab:40-44.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَفَأَصْفاكُمْ): "He singled you out and set you apart." Originally, taṣfiya means "purifying." Here, however, it is imbued with the meaning "set you apart," because of the connection of "sons" (البنين) with it. In al-Asās: "Figuratively: aṣfaytuhu l-mawadda and aṣfaytuhu bi-l-birr — I preferred him and singled him out. «أفأصفاكم ربكم بالبنين». And aṣfā ʿiyālahu bi-shayʾin yasīr means he satisfied them with a little. The hunter came upon a poor catch (khafq) and gave his children the ghubayrāʾ (a drink) as their share (aṣfā). Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
أو يصادف خفقا يصفهم ... بعتيق الخشل دون الطعام
(Or he comes upon a poor catch and gives them old khashal [dry dates] instead of food.)
And: he is my ṣafiyy (chosen friend) from among my brothers, and they are my aṣfiyāʾ. And ṣāfaytuhu: the two are khalīlān mutaṣāfiyān (close friends who treat each other sincerely)."
(صَرَّفْنا): "We made clear and explained." In the intensive form (with shadda) it has many meanings. One says ṣarrafahu in the sense of ṣarafahu with emphasis; ṣarrafa l-shayʾ means he sold it; ṣarrafa l-darāhim means he exchanged them; ṣarrafa l-khamr means he drank it ṣarfan, that is, unmixed; ṣarrafa l-kalām means he derived some of it from some other part; ṣarrafahu fī l-amr means he entrusted the matter to him; ṣarrafa l-māʾ means he made it flow; and ṣarrafa Allāhu l-riyāḥ means Allah made the winds flow from one direction to another.

* I'rab:
(أَفَأَصْفاكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ بِالْبَنِينَ وَاتَّخَذَ مِنَ الْمَلائِكَةِ إِناثاً): The hamza is for interrogation. In truth, this interrogative has the sense of refutation by denunciation (inkār ibṭālī), which implies that what follows it did not occur and that whoever claims it is lying; its meaning is reproach, rebuke, and also negation, that is, "He did not do that." أصفاكم is a past verb; the kāf is its object, and it is conjoined to an omitted clause that is implied according to the context. ربكم is the agent. بالبنين is attached to أصفاكم. واتخذ من الملائكة إناثا is conjoined to أصفاكم; it is a verb with a latent agent; من الملائكة is the second object of اتخذ, and إناثا is the first object. It is also possible that the clause اتخذ من الملائكة إناثا is a ḥāl (circumstantial) clause, the wāw being the wāw of ḥāl with qad implied.
(إِنَّكُمْ لَتَقُولُونَ قَوْلًا عَظِيماً): inna and its noun; the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); the clause تقولون is its predicate; قولا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and عظيما is an adjective.
(وَلَقَدْ صَرَّفْنا فِي هذَا الْقُرْآنِ لِيَذَّكَّرُوا وَما يَزِيدُهُمْ إِلَّا نُفُوراً): The wāw is a conjunction; the lām prepares for an oath; قد is a particle of certainty; صرفنا is a verb and agent, and its object is omitted, that is, "parables, admonitions, wise sayings, stories, reports, commands and prohibitions"; the pronoun was omitted because it is known. في هذا is attached to صرفنا, and القرآن is a badal (substitute). The lām is the lām of purpose; يذكروا is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied أن after the lām of purpose. The wāw is the wāw of ḥāl; ما is negative; يزيدهم is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; إلا is a particle of restriction; نفورا is the second object of يزيدهم.
(قُلْ لَوْ كانَ مَعَهُ آلِهَةٌ كَما يَقُولُونَ): قل is an imperative verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; لو is conditional; معه is an adverbial attached to an omitted predicate of the fronted kāna; آلهة is its postponed noun; وكما يقولون is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), that is, "a being similar to what they say."
(إِذاً لَابْتَغَوْا إِلى ذِي الْعَرْشِ سَبِيلًا): إذن is a particle of response and consequence, inoperative, indicating that what follows it, namely لابتغوا, is an answer to the statement of the polytheists. The lām occurs in the apodosis of لو. The clause ابتغوا has no grammatical position; the wāw is the agent; إلى ذي العرش is attached to ابتغوا, or to an omitted element as a ḥāl from سبيلا; and سبيلا is the object of ابتغوا.
(سُبْحانَهُ وَتَعالى عَمَّا يَقُولُونَ عُلُوًّا كَبِيراً): سبحانه is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, and it has been discussed many times. وتعالى is conjoined to what the maṣdar implies, the estimate being "He is exalted above (tanazzaha) and is high above (taʿālā)"; it is a past verb, and عما is attached to it; the clause يقولون is the ṣila (relative clause); علوا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq because it is a maṣdar standing in the place of al-taʿālī; and كبيرا is an adjective.
(تُسَبِّحُ لَهُ السَّماواتُ السَّبْعُ وَالْأَرْضُ وَمَنْ فِيهِنَّ): تسبح is an imperfect verb, and له is attached to it; السموات is the agent and السبع is an adjective; والأرض is conjoined to السموات; ومن is conjoined to السموات and الأرض; and فيهن is attached to an omitted element which is the ṣila of من.
(وَإِنْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ إِلَّا يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِهِ وَلكِنْ لا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ): The wāw is a conjunction; إن is negative; من is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition; شيء is genitive in form and nominative in position, and it was permissible to begin with it because of the preceding negation; إلا is a particle of restriction; يسبح is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he," and the clause is the khabar (predicate) of شيء; بحمده is a ḥāl, that is, "engaged in praise of Him." As for ولكن: the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl and لكن is an inoperative particle of rectification; لا is negative; تفقهون is an imperfect verb and agent; and تسبيحهم is the direct object.
(إِنَّهُ كانَ حَلِيماً غَفُوراً): inna and its noun; the clause كان is its predicate; the noun of كان is latent; حليما is the first predicate of كان and غفورا is its second predicate.

* Rhetoric:
In the words of Him the Exalted «وإن من شيء إلا يسبح بحمده ولكن لا تفقهون تسبيحهم» there is the figure of tankīt (the pointed choice). It was mentioned earlier: the speaker intends to mention one thing rather than another that could take its place, for a subtle point in the thing mentioned which makes its use preferable to the alternative. He specified "you understand deeply" (tafqahūn) rather than "you know" (taʿlamūn), because understanding (fiqh) adds something to knowledge: it is the handling of the thing known after knowing it, and the derivation of rulings from it. What the meaning of the speech requires is deep understanding of the recognition of praise from dumb animals, plants, inanimate things, and everything that falls under the word "thing" from among what has no reason and cannot speak, since the praise of such things consists merely in their existence, which points to the power and wisdom of their Creator.

dervis-irab:45-47.t:
* I'rab:
(وَإِذا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ جَعَلْنا بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ حِجاباً مَسْتُوراً) The wāw is resumptive. إذا is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition. قرأت القرآن: verb, agent and direct object (mafʿūl bihi); the clause is annexed to إذا. جعلنا: verb and agent. بينك: the adverb, attached to an omitted element; it is the second direct object. وبين الذين لا يؤمنون is conjoined to the first adverb. The clause لا يؤمنون is a ṣila (relative clause). بالآخرة: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يؤمنون. حجابا is the first direct object of جعلنا, and مستورا is an adjective (naʿt) of حجابا. It is also permissible that مستورا be taken in its ordinary sense, i.e. "not seen, hence concealed"; and it is permissible that it be a passive participle with the sense of an active one, i.e. "concealing you from them so that they do not see you". He means those who tried to assassinate the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
(وَجَعَلْنا عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ أَكِنَّةً أَنْ يَفْقَهُوهُ وَفِي آذانِهِمْ وَقْراً) جعلنا: verb and agent. على قلوبهم is the second direct object of جعلنا, and أكنة is the first direct object of جعلنا. أن يفقهوه is in the position of the accusative as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), i.e. "out of aversion to their understanding it"; it is also permissible that it be accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "from their understanding it". The preposition and its genitive noun are attached to أكنة, because it contains the sense of preventing understanding, as though it had been said "and We prevented them from understanding it". وفي آذانهم وقرا is conjoined to His words على قلوبهم أكنة.
(وَإِذا ذَكَرْتَ رَبَّكَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَحْدَهُ وَلَّوْا عَلى أَدْبارِهِمْ نُفُوراً) The wāw is a conjunction, and إذا is an adverb of future time; the clause ذكرت is annexed to it. ذكرت: verb and agent. ربك: direct object. في القرآن: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to ذكرت. وحده is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because it has the force of an indefinite, i.e. "alone". The clause ولوا has no grammatical position. على أدبارهم: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. نفورا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), because it has the sense of ولوا, i.e. it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) of it. It may also be parsed as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi. Abū al-Baqāʾ parsed it as a ḥāl, i.e. "fleeing", in which case it would be the plural of nāfir.
(نَحْنُ أَعْلَمُ بِما يَسْتَمِعُونَ بِهِ إِذْ يَسْتَمِعُونَ إِلَيْكَ) نحن is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and أعلم the khabar (predicate). بما: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أعلم. The clause يستمعون is a ṣila. به: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يستمعون; the bāʾ is causal, and the meaning is "what they listen to on account of it", namely mocking you and the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "به is in the position of a ḥāl, as we say يستمعون بالهزء, i.e. 'mockingly'." But there is some strain in this. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: the bāʾ has the sense of the lām. إذ is an adverb of past time, attached to أعلم, and the clause يستمعون إليك is annexed to the adverb. (وَإِذْ هُمْ نَجْوى) is conjoined to إذ and enters into its ruling, so it too is an adverb of أعلم, i.e. "and of what they confer secretly about, when they are [people of] private counsel". هم is the mubtadaʾ and نجوى the khabar, with an omitted muḍāf (the possessor of); it is also possible that نجوى is the plural of نجي, in which case there is no need to posit an omitted muḍāf before the khabar.
(إِذْ يَقُولُ الظَّالِمُونَ إِنْ تَتَّبِعُونَ إِلَّا رَجُلًا مَسْحُوراً) إذ يقول is a badal (substitute) of إذ هم نجوى or of إذ يستمعون إليك. يقول الظالمون: imperfect verb and agent. إن is negative. تتبعون: imperfect verb, nominative, and the wāw is the agent. إلا is a particle of restriction. رجلا is the direct object, and مسحورا is an adjective of رجلا.

* Benefits:
An interesting discussion of وحده:
Know that «وحده» has not been used except in the accusative, apart from what has come anomalously. They say: هو نسيج وحده, عيير وحده and جحيش وحده. As for نسيج وحده, it is praise; its origin is that when a garment is fine, no one else can be woven on its loom, so it is as if he said "the weave of his own singularity". This is said of a man who is singled out for excellence. As for عيير وحده and جحيش وحده, عيير is the diminutive of عير, which is the donkey (said of both the wild and the domestic), and جحيش is the donkey's foal; this is blame, said of a man who is pleased with his own opinion, who does not mix with anyone in an opinion and does not take part in anyone's assistance; its meaning is that he is alone in serving himself. As for your saying جاء وحده, وحده is a ḥāl from the latent agent of جاء. It is definite by annexation to the pronoun, so it is interpreted as an indefinite derived from its wording or its meaning, i.e. "single" or "alone". You say مررت به وحده and مررت بهم وحدهم; وحده is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, as though it had the meaning of إيحاد, coming with the augment letters dropped, as if you had said "I singled him out in my passing, a singling-out" (أوحدته بمروري إيحادا), or إيحاد in the sense of موحد, i.e. "alone". So when you say مررت به وحده it is as if you had said مررت به منفردا. According to Sībawayh it can refer to the agent and to the object.
Al-Zajjāj held that وحده is a maṣdar and refers to the agent and not the object; so when you say مررت به منفردا it is as if you had said "I singled him out in my passing, a singling-out" (أفردته بمروري إفرادا).
Yūnus said: when you say مررت به وحده it stands in the position of موحدا and منفردا, and you make it refer to the one passed by. Yūnus has another view on it: that وحده means على حياله ("on his own"), and على حياله is in the position of an adverbial; when an adverbial is an adjective or ḥāl, an established (mustaqirr) element is posited in it that governs the adverbial, and that mustaqirr is the first.

dervis-irab:1-8.t:
* Vocabulary:
(سُبْحانَ): a proper noun of a genus (ʿalam jins) denoting glorification and sanctification. It is accusative by an omitted verb whose mention is abandoned, its implied form being "I glorify Allah, subḥānahu" or "I glorified Allah, subḥāna", that is, it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object). Its meaning is "how far removed is the One who has this power from all deficiencies", and for that reason it is used only of Him, the Exalted.
(أَسْرى): sarā means "he travelled (sāra) by night". Both [asrā and sarā] are intransitive; the verbal noun (maṣdar) of the first is al-isrāʾ and the verbal noun of the second is al-sarā, with ḍamma on the sīn.
(مَرَّتَيْنِ): the dual of marra. In al-Qāmūs: "marra, marran and murūran: he passed, went and continued; marrahu and marra bihi: he passed over him; and imtarra bihi and ʿalayhi is like marra. And al-marra is a single act; the plural is marr, mirār and marar (both with kasra) and murūr (with ḍamma). 'I met him dhāta marra' [once]; it is used only adverbially."
(فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ): in al-Qāmūs: "al-jaws, with jīm, is seeking something thoroughly, and going back and forth among the houses and dwellings in a raid and roaming through them, like al-jawsān and al-ijtiyās; its verb pattern is qāla [i.e. jāsa, yajūsu]. And khilāl al-diyār has two analyses: first, that it is a singular noun meaning 'the middle'; second, that it is the plural of khalal, like jabal/jibāl and jamal/jimāl."
Al-Jawharī said: "al-jaws is the verbal noun of jāsū khilāla l-diyār, that is, they went through them seeking what was in them, as a man 'jaws' reports, that is, seeks them out." Al-Harawī in al-Gharībayn reported from al-Azharī that the meaning of jāsū is "they trampled". It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that one says "I left so-and-so jaws, yajūsu, yaḥūsu and yadūsu the sons of so-and-so", that is, he lays them waste [Translator's note: the printed text has yaḍuʾuhum, "he lights them up", which is apparently a misprint for a verb of trampling; translated as the context requires].
Abū ʿUbayd said: "every place you mixed with and trod upon, you have jus-tahu and ḥus-tahu."
(الْكَرَّةَ): victory and dominion (dawla). Originally it is a verbal noun from karra, as in "karrara", meaning "he returned"; then it came to be used to express dominion, subjugation and victory.
(نَفِيراً): al-nafīr is one who goes out (yanfiru) with a man from his people. It is also said to be the plural of nafar, like al-ʿabīd and al-maʿīz. It has several analyses: first, that it is a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, "one who goes out" (nāfir); second, that it is the plural of nafar like ʿabīd; third, that it is a verbal noun, that is, "going out more against the enemies". We have already mentioned that when nūn and fāʾ are the first and second radicals of a word, they indicate going out and passing through.
(يتبروا): al-tatbīr is destruction.
(حَصِيراً): a place of confinement, a prison. Labīd said:
ومقامه غلب الرجال كأنهم ... جن لدى باب الحصير قيام
(His place of standing: mighty men, as if they were jinn standing at the door of the prison.)
Al-Ḥasan said: it means "a mat" (firāsh), and also from him: it is taken from al-ḥaṣr (confinement). What appears [correct] is that it is "besieging" them, that is, encompassing them from all their sides. So ḥaṣīr means "possessing confinement" (dhāt ḥaṣr); for if it were for intensiveness, it would have to take the tāʾ, since it is applied to a feminine, as one says raḥīma and ʿalīma. But it is in the sense of relation (nisba), like His saying "the heaven will be split by it" (al-samāʾ munfaṭir bihi), that is, possessing a splitting.

* I'rab:
(سُبْحانَ الَّذِي أَسْرى بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى الَّذِي بارَكْنا حَوْلَهُ) سبحان is a mafʿūl muṭlaq of an omitted verb, whose discussion has already been given in the Vocabulary section. الذي is a muḍāf ilayhi (genitive), and the clause أسرى is its ṣila (relative clause). بعبده is attached to أسرى, and ليلا is an adverb attached to أسرى; the secret of mentioning it, although al-sarā occurs only at night, will come in the Rhetoric section. بعبده is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أسرى, and ليلا is an adverb of time also attached to أسرى. من المسجد is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), that is, "beginning"; and إلى المسجد الأقصى is also a ḥāl, that is, "ending at the mosque". الأقصى is a naʿt (adjective) of المسجد, and الذي is a second naʿt; باركنا is the ṣila, being a verb and agent, and حوله is an adverb attached to باركنا.
(لِنُرِيَهُ مِنْ آياتِنا إِنَّهُ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ) The lām is for causation, and نريه is an imperfect verb, accusative by an implied أن; its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "we"; the hā is a direct object. It is better to make the preposition and its genitive noun the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "and that is so that We may show him". من آياتنا is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to نريه; من is a preposition of partitiveness. إن and its noun; هو is a mubtadaʾ or a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and السميع is the khabar of هو or the khabar of إن, and البصير is a second khabar. The secret of these shifts of person (iltifātāt) will come in the Rhetoric section.
(وَآتَيْنا مُوسَى الْكِتابَ وَجَعَلْناهُ هُدىً لِبَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ) The wāw is resumptive, or conjoined to the clause سبحان الذي أسرى. نا is the agent, موسى is the first direct object and الكتاب the second direct object. جعلناه هدى is a verb and agent; the hā is the first direct object and هدى the second direct object. لبني is attached to هدى, and إسرائيل is a muḍāf ilayhi.
(أَلَّا تَتَّخِذُوا مِنْ دُونِي وَكِيلًا) It is permissible for أن to be a maṣdarī particle, accusative together with what follows it by removal of the preposition, that is, "so that you do not take", with the preposition and its genitive noun attached to كتبنا [Translator's note: this verb does not occur in the verse; the author evidently has in mind an implied "We decreed" or similar]; and it may be explicative (mufassira), because the "giving" contains the sense of saying without its letters. لا is prohibitive, and تتخذوا is an imperfect verb jussive by لا; وكيلا is the first direct object of تتخذوا, and من دوني is the second direct object of تتخذوا [Translator's note: so the source; the order of the "first" and "second" objects is as printed].
(ذُرِّيَّةَ مَنْ حَمَلْنا مَعَ نُوحٍ إِنَّهُ كانَ عَبْداً شَكُوراً) ذرية:
The statements of the i'rab scholars about its case, which all the readers agree is accusative, were confused. It was said: accusative as a specification of praise (ikhtiṣāṣ), and with this al-Zamakhsharī began; it was said: as a vocative; it was said: a badal of وكيلا; it was said: a second direct object of تتخذوا; though the soul is not at rest with any one of them, and Allah knows best. من is annexed to ذرية (muḍāf), and حملنا is a ṣila; مع is an adverb of place attached to حملنا, and نوح is a muḍāf ilayhi. إن and its noun; كان is a defective past verb, its noun a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; عبدا is its khabar and شكورا an adjective. Among the things that favour the i'rab of ذرية as ikhtiṣāṣ or vocative is al-Zamakhsharī's statement in the i'rab of the clause "إنه كان عبدا شكورا", that it is a causal clause for their being singled out as the children of those carried with Nūḥ, as if it were said: "Do not take any guardian besides Me and do not associate anything with Me, because Nūḥ, peace be upon him, was a thankful servant, and you are the offspring of those who believed in him and were carried with him; so make him your example, as your forefathers made him their example." This is an insight of al-Zamakhsharī that draws attention and deserves admiration.
(وَقَضَيْنا إِلى بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ فِي الْكِتابِ) The wāw is a conjunction, and قضينا is a verb and agent. إلى بني إسرائيل is attached to قضينا. قضينا is originally a verb that governs its object directly, but here it is made transitive by إلى because it includes the meaning of "We revealed" (awḥaynā). The meaning of قضينا is "We informed and told", or "We ruled and completed"; the original sense of al-qaḍāʾ is making something firm and being finished with it. It is also said [to mean] "We revealed", and the phrase إلى بني إسرائيل indicates this; for if it meant informing and telling, He would have said "qaḍaynā banī Isrāʾīl"; if it meant "We ruled", He would have said "ʿalā banī Isrāʾīl"; and if it meant "We completed", He would have said "li-banī Isrāʾīl". في الكتاب is a ḥāl, and what is meant by it is the Torah.
(لَتُفْسِدُنَّ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ) The lām is the answer to an omitted oath, or [it is said that] the decisive decree is treated as an oath, as if it were said: "and We swore: you will surely cause corruption". تفسدن is an imperfect verb which is declinable (muʿrab) because the emphatic heavy nūn is not directly attached to it; the sign of its nominative case is the presence of the nūn, [the nūn of the plural being] omitted because of the succession of nūns, and the wāw of the group, omitted because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, is the agent; the original is لتفسدونن, and parallels have already been given. في الأرض is attached to تفسدن, and مرتين is accusative as an adverb (ẓarfiyya). Abū l-Baqāʾ analysed it as a mafʿūl muṭlaq, as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as being itself a verbal noun in which something of a different genus works. The meaning of "twice" will come in the Benefits section.
(وَلَتَعْلُنَّ عُلُوًّا كَبِيراً) The wāw is a conjunction, and ولتعلن is conjoined to لتفسدن and is similar to it in its i'rab. علوا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq and كبيرا an adjective.
(فَإِذا جاءَ وَعْدُ أُولاهُما بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكُمْ عِباداً لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, and إذا is an adverb of the future containing the meaning of condition; the clause جاء is annexed to by the adverb. وعد is the agent, and أولاهما is annexed to وعد. Since a "promise" in its absolute sense is specific to good, it is necessary to assume an omitted muḍāf, that is, "the promise of punishment for the first of the two". The clause بعثنا has no grammatical position, because it is the answer of a non-jussive condition. عليكم is attached to بعثنا, and عبادا is a direct object. أولي is an adjective of عبادا, and it is one of the five nouns, in the sense of "possessors" (aṣḥāb); بأس is a muḍāf ilayhi and شديد an adjective of بأس.
(فَجاسُوا خِلالَ الدِّيارِ وَكانَ وَعْداً مَفْعُولًا) The fāʾ is a conjunction, and جاسوا is conjoined to بعثنا. خلال is an adverb of place attached to جاسوا, and الديار is a muḍāf ilayhi. The wāw is a conjunction, and كان is conjoined to al-jaws; its noun is a pronoun referring back to al-jaws or to the promise of punishment, and وعدا is the khabar of كان, and مفعولا an adjective of وعدا.
(ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الْكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ) ثم is a conjunction of delay, and رددنا is a verb and agent. لكم is attached to رددنا, and الكرة is a direct object; عليهم is attached to الكرة, that is, "victory over them", or it is a ḥāl from it.
(وَأَمْدَدْناكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ وَجَعَلْناكُمْ أَكْثَرَ نَفِيراً) وأمددناكم is conjoined to رددنا; it is a verb, agent and direct object. بأموال is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أمددناكم, and بنين is conjoined to أموال. جعلناكم is a verb, agent and direct object; أكثر is a second direct object and نفيرا a tamyīz (specification).
(إِنْ أَحْسَنْتُمْ أَحْسَنْتُمْ لِأَنْفُسِكُمْ وَإِنْ أَسَأْتُمْ فَلَها) إن is conditional, and أحسنتم is a verb and agent, in the position of the jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), and the second أحسنتم is its apodosis. وإن أسأتم is conjoined to إن أحسنتم; the fāʾ is the connector of the apodosis, and لها is attached to an omitted khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "so your doing evil [is] against it". Analogy would require that He say "fa-ʿalayhā", but he departed to the lām for symmetry with "li-anfusikum"; it was also said that the lām is in the sense of ʿalā, that is, "fa-ʿalayhā", as in the verse of ʿAntara:
فخرّ صريعا لليدين وللفم
(So he fell down, struck, upon his hands and upon his mouth.)
(فَإِذا جاءَ وَعْدُ الْآخِرَةِ لِيَسُوؤُا وُجُوهَكُمْ) The fāʾ is a conjunction and إذا an adverb of the future; جاء وعد is a verb and agent, and الآخرة is annexed to وعد; He meant the last time. ليسوءوا: the lām is for causation, and "yasūʾū" [Translator's note: the source writes ويسيئوا, "yusīʾū", which is evidently a slip for the verb of the verse] is an imperfect verb accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; it is attached to the omitted answer of إذا, that is, "We sent them so that they would disfigure", and the answer of the first إذا indicates the answer. وجوهكم is a direct object. The meaning is "so that they make your faces show distress and the features darkened".
(وَلِيَدْخُلُوا الْمَسْجِدَ كَما دَخَلُوهُ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ) وليدخلوا is conjoined to ليسوءوا, that is, it is attached to the omitted "We sent them". المسجد is accusative by extension (ʿalā l-siʿa). كما is accusative as a maṣdar, that is, "an entry like their entry", and أول مرة is accusative as an adverb.
(وَلِيُتَبِّرُوا ما عَلَوْا تَتْبِيراً) وليتبروا is conjoined to ليسوءوا, and the wāw of the group is the agent; ما is the direct object of ليتبروا, that is, "so that they destroy everything they overcame and took control of". It is also permissible to make ما a maṣdarī adverbial particle (ṭarfiyya), with the object of يتبروا omitted, and perhaps this is better, to give room for the imagination to picture the extent of their destruction of crops and offspring during the period of their dominance over the land; the adverb would then be attached to يتبروا. تتبيرا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.
(عَسى رَبُّكُمْ أَنْ يَرْحَمَكُمْ وَإِنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا وَجَعَلْنا جَهَنَّمَ لِلْكافِرِينَ حَصِيراً) عسى is a past verb of the verbs of hope; it takes a nominative noun and an accusative khabar. ربكم is its noun, and أن with what follows it is in the position of the accusative as its khabar. The wāw is a conjunction, and إن is conditional; عدتم is a past verb and agent, in the position of the jussive as the protasis; عدنا is a past verb and agent, in the position of the jussive as the apodosis. جعلنا is conjoined to عدنا; نا is the agent, جهنم the first direct object; للكافرين is attached to حصيرا, and حصيرا is the second direct object. This is if we consider حصيرا a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil; but if we consider it a rigid noun, that is, the known place of confinement, then للكافرين would be a ḥāl from it.

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain several kinds of rhetoric, which we set out as follows.

1- Mention (al-dhikr):
The mention of "night", although al-sarā occurs only at night, admits two explanations:
(a) The first: that since al-isrāʾ indicates two things, one being travel and the other its being at night, it was desired to single out one of them for mention, to fix it in the mind of the addressee and to alert him that it is the intended point of the mention. This subtle point was already indicated in His saying "And Allah said: Do not take two gods; He is only one God", for the noun that carries duality indicates it and also the genus, and likewise the singular; so attention was drawn because one of the two meanings, duality, is the one intended.
(b) The second: the indication, through making "night" indefinite, that its duration was short, because indefiniteness indicates partiality. This is unlike if it had been said "asrā bi-ʿabdihi al-layl", for the construction with the definite article would indicate that the travel covered all parts of the night.

2- Connection and disconnection (al-waṣl wa l-faṣl):
Among the arts hard to attain, which weigh heavily on whoever seeks them, are disconnection and connection. For the reader feels that between the verse of al-isrāʾ and His saying "And We gave Moses the Book" to the end of the verse there is a great disparity in outward appearance, until, when he reflects and contemplates, he finds the connection between the two actions. For He, the Exalted, reported that He made Muḥammad ﷺ travel by night to the Holy Land to show him of His signs and to send him to His servants, just as He made Moses travel from Egypt to Madyan when he left fearful and watchful, and made him and his son-in-law Shuʿayb travel to the Holy Land to show him of His signs and send him to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and gave him the Book. This is the connection between the two mentioned sections. As for the connection between His saying: "offspring of those We carried with Noah" and what precedes it, it is a reminder to the Children of Israel of the first of His favours, Mighty and Majestic, upon them, in the salvation of their forefathers with Noah in the ark from drowning; for had their forefathers not been saved, they would not have existed. It is as though the abundant favours upon them were a chain of successive links, the first of which was the salvation of their forefathers from the drowning of the Flood that covered the whole world, and the last of which was their salvation from drowning when the sea was split for them so that Pharaoh, his soldiers and his chiefs would be drowned and they would be saved. It then followed that they should thank the One who bestowed these blessings and kindnesses on them, and take Noah, their greatest ancestor, as an example, who was a thankful servant. Is not the son the secret of his father? But these people are unique in their ingratitude, denial, disdain for favour and meeting good deeds with evil ones.

3- Shift of person (al-iltifāt):
We have spoken of iltifāt much in this book, and many examples of it have preceded. In this verse, the verse of al-isrāʾ, iltifāt succeeded itself many times despite the brevity of its text and the closeness of its two ends. He first said "Glory be to Him who made His servant travel (asrā)" in the singular third person; then He said "which We blessed (bāraknā)" in the first person plural; then He said "He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing" in the singular third person. Had the speech followed the course of the first, it would have been "Glory be to Him who made His servant travel by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, around which He blessed, to show him of His signs; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing". All of this is dependent on asrā. When the conjoined was made to differ from what it is conjoined to by moving from one form to another, this was an expansion of speech, an artistry in it and a variation of its styles. The benefit of it, besides refreshing the vigour of the mind, making it present and drawing its attention to the presentation of truths full of lessons and admonitions, is that when He began the speech with subḥānahu, He followed it with His saying "alladhī asrā", since it is not permissible to say "alladhī asraynā". When He used the singular form, while Allah the Exalted is the greatest of the great, and the one most worthy of being addressed in the form appropriate to the great in himself, which is the plural, He made up for the first by the second and said "bāraknā"; then He said "li-nuriyahu min āyātinā", which followed the pattern of "bāraknā"; then He said "innahu huwa", conjoined to asrā, and that is an intermediate position of attribute, because hearing and seeing are two attributes in which others share with Him, setting aside the difference between the two hearings and the two seeings; this is an intermediate state. So by them He moved from addressing the great in himself to addressing an absent party. These are far-reaching aims, of lofty purpose, whose depth is not fathomed and whose import is not grasped except by the naturally gifted.

* Benefits:
1- The prepositions "min" and "ilā":
The preposition "min" has many meanings, to which one can refer in Mughnī l-labīb and other lengthy books of grammar. But we wish to point to its main meaning occurring in the verse of al-isrāʾ, which is the beginning (ibtidāʾ), that is, the beginning of the spatial limit, by agreement of all the grammarians, Basran and Kufan, as shown by the end of the limit after it, which is His saying "ilā l-masjid al-aqṣā". As for the beginning of the temporal limit, the grammarians differed: the Kufans affirmed it, and among the Basrans al-Mubarrad, al-Akhfash and Ibn Durustawayh affirmed it, and this is the correct view because of its occurrence in the Noble Book, which is His saying "from the first day, [it is] more worthy that you stand therein"; in the Ḥadīth, which is the saying of Anas "so we were rained upon from Friday to Friday"; and in poetry, which is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī, describing swords:
تخيرن من أزمان يوم حليمة ... إلى اليوم قد جربن كل التجارب
(They were chosen from the times of the Day of Ḥalīma until today; they have been tried in every trial.)
As for the preposition "ilā", it indicates the end of the limit, spatial and temporal. An example in place is "ilā l-masjid al-aqṣā", and an example in time is "then complete the fast until (ilā) the night". "Ilā" has seven other meanings that Mughnī l-labīb and others relate. Among the meanings of "ilā" that are problematic is again the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī, excusing himself to al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir:
فلا تتركني بالوعيد كأنني ... إلى الناس مطلي به القار أجرب
(So do not leave me with threats, as if I were, among the people, a mangy [camel] smeared with pitch.)
It is mentioned in al-Mughnī that here it means "fī" (in), which is odd. Al-Damāmīnī said: "ilā is attached to an omitted ḥāl from the noun of ka'anna, that is, 'as if I were hated by the people because of the threat, like a mangy camel smeared with pitch', that is, pitch was put on it or it was characterised by it." Al-Damāmīnī overlooked the inversion in "muṭlī bihi l-qār", or else he strained it to make muṭlī mean "hated"; for pitch is smeared on, and does not itself smear; hence it is necessary to return to the opinion of Ibn Hishām, that ilā means fī and that the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl, that is, "as if I, being among the people, were a camel smeared with pitch, and hated".

2- The meaning of "twice":
The commentators differed in interpreting the two times mentioned in His saying "you will surely cause corruption in the earth twice". Some held that the first time was the killing of Zakariyyā and the imprisonment of Jeremiah, and the second the killing of Yaḥyā and the attempt to kill ʿĪsā. Al-Bayḍāwī said: "The first of them was opposing the rulings of the Torah and the killing of Shaʿyā, and it was said Jeremiah; the second was the killing of Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā and the attempt to kill ʿĪsā, peace be upon them." Yet the corruption of the Jews in the earth cannot be limited to two times; the Noble Qur'an mentioned "twice" only as a quick example of their countless corruption, which continues throughout the ages. One may refer to the longer works for this purpose.

dervis-irab:48-52.t:
* Vocabulary:
(رُفاتاً): al-rufāt is what has been pounded and crushed excessively; it is a singular noun for the parts of that crushed thing. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is dust, which is supported by the fact that "dust and bones" (ترابا وعظاما) recurs in the Qur'an. One says رفت الشيء يرفته (with kasra), i.e. he broke it; and the pattern فعال predominantly indicates breaking into pieces, like الحطام, الرقاق and الفتات. In al-Qāmūs and Tāj al-ʿArūs: «رفته يرفته ويرفته: he broke it and pounded it; and it broke and was pounded, both intransitive and transitive; and it was cut off, like ارفتّ ارفتاتا in all these senses; and رُفات on the pattern of غراب means debris, and on the pattern of صرد: chaff, and that which breaks everything, i.e. smashes it.» In al-Asās: «وفي ملاعبهن رفات المسك (in their playing-places is crushed musk), i.e. its fragments. It is said of one who has done something from which he cannot extricate himself: "the hyena crushes the bones and does not know the size of its rump; it eats them, then their passing becomes hard for it." And figuratively: he is the one who restored noble deeds, revived their remains and resurrected their dead.»
(فَسَيُنْغِضُونَ): i.e. they move their heads. In al-Mukhtār: نغض رأسه (of the pattern of نصر and جلس) means it moved; and أنغض رأسه means he moved it like one who is amazed at something, and from this comes His words, the Exalted: «فسينغضون إليك رؤوسهم». And نغض فلان رأسه means he moved it, being both transitive and intransitive. In al-Lisān: one says أنغض رأسه ينغضها, i.e. he moved it up and down, an inghāḍ, and he is a munghiḍ. As for the triliteral نغض ينغض, and ينغض with fatḥa or ḍamma, its meaning is "he moved" and it is not transitive.

* I'rab:
(انْظُرْ كَيْفَ ضَرَبُوا لَكَ الْأَمْثالَ فَضَلُّوا فَلا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَبِيلًا) انظر: imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". كيف: an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. ضربوا: verb and agent. لك: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to ضربوا. الأمثال: direct object. فضلوا is conjoined to ضربوا, the fāʾ being a conjunction. لا is negative. يستطيعون سبيلا: verb, agent and direct object. (وَقالُوا أَإِذا كُنَّا عِظاماً وَرُفاتاً) The wāw is a conjunction. قالوا: verb and agent. The hamza is for rejecting interrogation and for deeming improbable what they ask about. إذا is an adverb of future time attached to an omitted element, its implied form being "will we be raised" or "will we be gathered, when we have become bones and crumbled dust"; مبعوثون indicates it. It cannot be attached to it [مبعوثون], because what follows inna does not act on what precedes it, and likewise what follows the interrogative does not act on what precedes it, and the two are combined here; the answer is the verb to which it was attached. كنا: kāna and its noun; عظاما is its khabar; ورفاتا is conjoined to عظاما. (أَإِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ خَلْقاً جَدِيداً) The hamza is for rejecting interrogation and deeming improbable, as above. إن and its noun, and the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); مبعوثون is the khabar of inna. خلقا is a ḥāl, i.e. "as created beings", or a mafʿūl muṭlaq derived from the meaning of the verb, not from its wording, i.e. "we will be raised with a new raising"; and جديدا is an adjective.
(قُلْ كُونُوا حِجارَةً أَوْ حَدِيداً) The clause كونوا حجارة is the content of what is said (maqūl al-qawl). كان and its noun, and حجارة is its khabar. أو is a conjunction, and حديدا is conjoined to حجارة. The command here means rendering them powerless, together with contempt. (أَوْ خَلْقاً مِمَّا يَكْبُرُ فِي صُدُورِكُمْ) أو is a conjunction; خلقا is conjoined to حجارة; مما is an adjective of خلقا; the clause يكبر is a ṣila; في صدوركم: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يكبر. (فَسَيَقُولُونَ مَنْ يُعِيدُنا قُلِ الَّذِي فَطَرَكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, and the sīn is a particle of futurity. يقولون: imperfect verb and agent. من: an interrogative noun in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ; the clause يعيدنا is the khabar. قل: imperative verb. الذي فطركم is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, its implied form being "will restore you"; or it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "He is the One who created you". The clause فطركم is a ṣila. أول مرة: an adverbial attached to فطركم. (فَسَيُنْغِضُونَ إِلَيْكَ رُؤُسَهُمْ وَيَقُولُونَ مَتى هُوَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, the sīn is for futurity. ينغضون: imperfect verb and agent. إليك: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to ينغضون, i.e. they move their heads up and down, in mockery and ridicule. رؤوسهم is the direct object. يقولون is conjoined to ينغضون. متى: an interrogative noun attached to an omitted element, a fronted khabar; and هو is a postponed mubtadaʾ, i.e. the resurrection.
(قُلْ عَسى أَنْ يَكُونَ قَرِيباً) عسى is among the verbs of hope; its noun is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "it". أن and what follows it are in the position of the accusative as the khabar of عسى. The noun of يكون is latent, its implied form being "it", and قريبا is its khabar. (يَوْمَ يَدْعُوكُمْ فَتَسْتَجِيبُونَ بِحَمْدِهِ) Regarding what this adverbial is attached to there are statements with which the soul is not at ease, because the closest to comprehension is that it be attached to the noun of kāna, i.e. the resurrection; but that is impossible grammatically, because a pronoun does not govern. So it is preferable to parse it as a badal of قريبا, or as attached to يكون according to the view of those who hold that incomplete verbs can have attachments. Abū al-Suʿūd, following Abū al-Baqāʾ, preferred that it be an adverbial of "remember" (اذكر), which is remote from the flow of the subject. The clause يدعوكم is annexed to the adverbial. فتستجيبون is conjoined to يدعوكم. بحمده: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, i.e. "praising". Al-Zamakhsharī said, and did well: «It is an exaggeration of their compliance with the resurrection, as you say to one whom you command to mount something burdensome to him and he refuses and resists: "You will mount it and you will be praising and thankful."» (وَتَظُنُّونَ إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا) The wāw is circumstantial (ḥāliyya). تظنون: imperfect verb, nominative, and an agent, i.e. "it will seem to you", because of the excess of the terror and dread you endure. إن is negative. لبثتم: verb and agent. إلا is a particle of restriction. قليلا is an adverbial attached to لبثتم, i.e. in this world; that is, you will deem short the length of your stay in this world and reckon it a day or part of a day. It is an adjective of an omitted time; it may also be an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "a brief stay".

* Rhetoric:
In His words, the Exalted, «قل كونوا حجارة أو حديدا أو خلقا مما يكبر في صدوركم» to the end of the verse, there are two arts of rhetoric:
1- The first is an art called al-tamkīn, which some call al-irṣād. Its reality is that the speaker prepares for his rhyme-word or the rhyming close of his phrase with a preparation in which the rhyme-word comes firmly placed, settled in its resting-place, neither jarring nor restless, so that the hearer knows that he meant حجارة أو حديدا by a pull from his heart and an inspiration from his inner voice, without hearing the rest of the verse. An example in poetry is the words of Abū al-Ṭayyib:
يا من يعز علينا أن نفارقهم ... وجداننا كل شيء بعدكم عدم
(O you from whom it is hard for us to part, our finding anything after you is nothingness.)
And al-Buḥturī on ʿUlwa al-Ḥalabiyya:
فليس الذي حللته بمحلل ... وليس الذي حرمته بحرام
(What you have declared permitted is not permitted, and what you have forbidden is not forbidden.)
And al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī said, in the old days:
كالاقحوان غداة غب سمائه ... جفت أعاليه وأسفله ندي
(Like the chamomile on the morning after its rain, its upper parts dry and its lower parts moist.)
زعم الهمام ولم أذقه بأنه ... يشفى بريّا ريقها العطش الصدي
(The chief claimed, though I did not taste it, that the parched thirst is healed by the fragrance of her saliva.)
Among the curiosities of this art is what is related, that al-Sirāj al-Warrāq, Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Jazzār and Ibn Nafīs the poet gathered, and a handsome youth passed by them. Al-Sirāj said:
شمائله تدل على اللطافة ... وريقته تنوب عن السّلافة
(His traits indicate gracefulness, and his saliva stands in for choice wine.)
Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Jazzār said:
وفي وجناته ورد ولكن ... عقارب صدغه منعت قطافه
(In his cheeks are roses, but the scorpions of his temple-locks prevent their picking.)
Ibn Nafīs said:
فلو ولي الخلافة ذو جمال ... لحق له بأن يعطى الخلافة
(Were a man of beauty to rule the caliphate, he would have the right to be given the caliphate.)
They cast the rhymes in all three firmly placed, as you see.
2- The second art in these two verses is al-takhyīr, which is that a piece of speech or a line of poetry is brought as a whole, parts of it being conjoined to others by a particle of choice, and it contains soundness of division, so that his speech covers the categories of the meaning the speaker has taken up. Look at the takhyīr in these two verses, the soundness of the division and the beauty of the ordering in the movement, in the manner of eloquence, from the lower to the higher, until He, glory be to Him, reached the utmost in the most concise allusion and sweetest expression, when after moving on from stone He said: «أو حديدا», moving from stone to what is harder and stronger than it; then after that He said: «أو خلقا مما يكبر في صدوركم», not confining them to one kind among the kinds. And picture, reader, after that how the meaning is completed and shines in the soul, a shining in which the soul is immersed: that is, you deem it improbable that Allah would renew your creation and return it to the state of life, to its moistness and tenderness, after you were dry bones; and that is your habit in denial, and your custom in obstinacy.
