It is related that some of the licentious sent Abū Tammām a bottle and said, 'Send me in this some of the water of reproach,' and Abū Tammām sent to him saying, 'If you send me a feather from the wing of humility, I will send you some of the water of reproach.' But the difference between these two similes could not have escaped Abū Tammām, for giving a wing to humility is not like giving water to reproach. A wing for humility is appropriate, for when a bird is weak or tired, it spreads its wing, lowers it, and throws itself on the ground; the human being too has wings, for his arms are his wings, and when he submits and is humbled he bows his head and lowers his arms; so at that point attributing the wing to humility is beautiful and the simile becomes an appropriate one. Water for reproach is not like that in appropriateness of simile."
This is what al-Ṣūlī and Ibn al-Athīr set down, and many critics of the fourth Islamic century commented on them, some supporting and some opposing. Al-Āmidī in his book al-Muwāzana took al-Ṣūlī's view, but on another basis of understanding, and faulted Abū Tammām for using metaphors similar to "the water of reproach." He said: "Among his rejected words and ugly metaphors is his saying:
يا دهر قوّمّ أخدعيك فقد ... أضججت هذا الأنام من خرقك
(O Time, straighten your two veins [akhdaʿayk], for you have made these people cry out because of your folly.)
and he said:
سأشكر فرجة الليت الرخي ... ولين أخادع الدهر الأبي
(I shall thank the opening of the soft lion... and the softness with which I deceive the proud Time.)
and he said:
أنزلته الأيام عن ظهرها ... من بعد إثبات رجله في الركاب
(The days brought him down from their back after he had set his foot in the stirrup.)
and he said:
كأنني حين جردت الرجاء له ... غضّا صببت به ماء على الزمن
(As though, when I stripped hope bare for him, tender, I poured water with it on the lame.)"
Then he said: "And the like of this, which you will find if you follow his poetry. So he gave Time, as you see, with the poor quality of these words, two neck veins and a hand cut off at the wrist, as if it were thrown down, untied, chokes on the noble and smiles; and the days are shod, and Time is piebald; and he gave the praised one a hand, and gave the days a back to ride, and Time as though water were poured on it."
Let us now consider "the water of reproach" in Abū Tammām: is it a natural expression? Is it an acceptable and approved expression? The unqualified use of "water" and its annexation to weeping first leaps to the mind with the immediate familiar image of water that is drunk, and water in seas, oceans and rivers, then rain water; but as soon as the word "weeping" is uttered the first meaning shrinks suddenly and contracts to a partial image, a few drops of tears. At any rate there is a connection that makes the image plausible. As for the water of reproach, there is absolutely no connection between water and reproach, and if the word "water" is released with its original and associative meanings, together with the word "reproach" and its associative meanings, no connection or common link among the partial images joins them; therefore the expression is cold and flawed, indicating nothing in the mind, because there is no connection between reproach and water. As for what al-Ṣūlī adduced from the Qur'an, it does not justify what he relied upon: the word "evil" was joined to the word "requital" and so evoked another, corresponding meaning, namely retaliation, which the Qur'an called "evil"; but the people of badīʿ try to cite the Qur'anic evidence to justify the craft of Abū Tammām and those who followed his way.
I found an opinion of al-Sakkākī in which he rejects Abū Tammām's saying. He says: "The takhyīliyya metaphor (imaginative metaphor) in it is separable from the metaphor by implication, and the author of al-Īḍāḥ denies the separability in it, on the ground that he may have likened reproach to a vessel of detested drink, so it would be a metaphor by implication, and the annexation of water is imaginative; or it is a simile of the kind 'the silver of water,' not a metaphor. He said: the common ground is that blame calms the heat of passion, just as water calms the burning of thirst." The excellent al-Jalabī said in his gloss on al-Muṭawwal: "There is something to consider here, because what is suitable for the lover is to claim that the heat of his passion is not calmed by reproach or by anything else, so how can he make that the ground of the simile?" End of his words.
In the book al-Kashkūl by al-ʿĀmilī I saw a long opinion, of which we cite the gist to complete the discussion. He said: "The verse has another interpretation, which I thought no one had preceded me to until I saw it in al-Tibyān, namely that the 'water of reproach' is of the kind of mushākala (assimilation) to the mention of the 'water of weeping.' Do not think that the lateness of the mention of the water of weeping prevents mushākala; they took pains in the words of Him the Exalted «فمنهم من يمشي على بطنه ومنهم من يمشي على رجلين», saying that the naming of crawling on the belly as 'walking' is for assimilation to what follows. This interpretation proceeds only on the assumption that the transmitted anecdote is not sound. Then I say: this interpretation is preferable to what the author of al-Īḍāḥ mentioned, for the two aspects he mentioned are extremely remote, since there is nothing in the verse indicating that the water is disliked, as the verifier al-Taftāzānī said in al-Muṭawwal, and the simile is not complete without it. As for what the author of al-Mathal al-Sāʾir mentioned, that the common ground is that reproach is speech with which the reproached is chided and it is specific to hearing, so Abū Tammām transferred it to what is specific to the throat, as though he said, 'Do not make me taste reproach,' and since hearing gulps reproach first as the throat gulps water it became as if likened to it — this is also an extremely remote aspect, as is not hidden; and it is strange of him to have made it close and to have overlooked the lack of fit between water and reproach. Some, however, answered al-Jalabī's objection to the words of the author of al-Īḍāḥ by saying that the poet's likening of reproach to water in calming the fire of passion is according to the belief of the blamers, that the heat of lovers' passion is calmed by the arrival of reproach, and is not according to his own belief; for perhaps his belief is that the fire of passion increases with reproach. Abū l-Shīṣ said:
أجد الملامة في هواك لذيذة ... حبا لذكرك فليلمني اللوّم
(I find reproach for loving you sweet, out of love for the mention of you, so let the blamers blame me.)
or that that fire is not affected by reproach at all, as another said:
جاءوا يرومون سلواني بلومهم ... عن الحبيب فراحوا مثلما جاءوا
(They came seeking my consolation by blaming me for the beloved, and they left as they came.)
So al-Jalabī's saying 'because what is suitable for the lover…' to the end is not sound, for the author of al-Īḍāḥ did not say that the simile is the lover's belief." Al-ʿĀmilī, the author of al-Kashkūl, added: "The author of al-Īḍāḥ's mention of the dislike in the drink is explicit that he is not content with this answer."
2- A embodied image of obedience to parents:
It is necessary to draw attention to the embodied image that the verse paints of obedience to parents and kindness to them, so that sons may reflect on it and fathom its hidden secret. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made it clear when a man complained to him about his father, that he took his wealth. He called for him, and there was an old man leaning on a staff, and he asked him. He said: "He was weak and I was strong, poor and I was rich, so I did not withhold anything of my wealth from him; today I am weak and he is strong, I am poor and he is rich, and he is stingy with his wealth towards me." Then he turned to his son, reciting:
غذوتك مولودا وعلتك يافعا ... تعل بما أدني إليك وتنهل
إذا ليلة نابتك بالشكو لم أبت ... لأجلك إلا ساهرا أتململ
كأني أنا المطروق دونك بالذي ... طرقت به دوني فعيني تهمل
فلما بلغت السنّ والغاية التي ... إليها مدى ما كنت فيك أؤمل
جعلت جزائي غلظة وفظاظة ... كأنك أنت المنعم المتفضل
فليتك إذ لم ترع حقّ أبوتي ... فعلت كما الجار المجاور يفعل
(I fed you as a newborn and supported you as a youth; you drank again and again of what I brought near to you. When a night of complaint befell you, I did not spend it for your sake except sleepless, tossing. It was as though I, not you, was the one struck by what struck you, so my eye streamed. Then when you reached the age and the goal to which my hopes for you extended, you made my reward harshness and rudeness, as though you were the benefactor, the bestower of favours. Would that, since you did not respect my right as a father, you had done as the neighbouring neighbour does.)
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ wept and said: "There is no stone or clod of earth that hears this but weeps." Then he said to the son: "You and your wealth belong to your father."
And on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar: that he saw a man in the circumambulation carrying his mother and saying:
إني لها مطية لا تذعر ... إذا الركاب نفرت لا تنفر
ما حملت وأرضعتني أكثر ... الله ربي ذو الجلال أكبر
(I am a mount for her that is not startled; when the mounts shy, I do not shy. What she carried and nursed me with is more. Allah is my Lord, Possessor of Majesty, Greater.)
"Do you think I have repaid her, Ibn ʿUmar?" He said: "No, not even for one groan."

* Benefits:
1- The discussion of «أف»:
The grammarians differed concerning the nouns of verbs (asmāʾ al-afʿāl): are they words standing in for the verbs, or for their meanings of events and times, or nouns of the maṣdars that stand in for verbs, or are they verbs? The sound view is that they are nouns of verbs and that they have no grammatical position. We have already presented their classes. We say that «أف» is a noun of an imperfect verb meaning "I am fed up," and in it there are forty dialectal forms. The sum of them is that the hamza is either with ḍamma, kasra or fatḥa. If it has ḍamma, there are twenty-two forms; the sum of their classification is that it is either bare of appendages or attached to an addition. The bare form is either with a silent end or a vowelled end; the vowelled is either doubled or lightened, and each of the two takes the three vowels on its end, with tanwīn and without it — these are twelve; the silent form is either doubled or lightened — these make fourteen. The appendages added to it are either the hāʾ of pause (hāʾ al-sakt) or a letter of prolongation. If it is the hāʾ of pause, the fāʾ takes three vowels doubled — these make seventeen. If it is a letter of prolongation, it is either wāw, yāʾ, or alif, and the fāʾ is doubled in them; and the alif is either full, or with pure imāla, or in between — these are five more with the seventeen. If it has kasra, there are eleven: the fāʾ with three vowels, lightened, with tanwīn and without it — these are six; the fāʾ with fatḥa and with kasra, doubled in both, with tanwīn and without — these are four forms; and the eleventh is أفي with imāla. If it has fatḥa, the fāʾ is doubled with fatḥa and kasra and tanwīn and its absence; the fifth is أف with sukūn; the sixth is أفي with imāla; and the seventh is أفاه with the hāʾ of pause. These seven complete the forty. Seven of these forms have been read: three in the mutawātir readings and four in the irregular readings. Ḥafṣ's reading, which is our reading, is أف with kasra and tanwīn, with doubling.

2- A glance at disobedience to parents:
Among what came regarding disobedience to parents is what is related of Jarīr: he was the most disobedient of people to his father, and his son Bilāl was the same. Jarīr disputed with Bilāl in speech, and he said to him: "The liar between me and you... is his mother." His mother turned to him and said: "Enemy of Allah, you say this to your father?" Jarīr said: "Leave him, for it is as if he heard it from me when I said it to my father."
Among those famous for disobedience to their parents is al-Ḥuṭayʾa, the poet who lived through both eras (mukhaḍram). He said, satirizing his father:
فنعم الشيخ أنت لدى المخازي ... وبئس الشيخ أنت لدى الفعال
جمعت اللؤم لا حيّاك ربي ... وأبواب السفاهة والضلال
(What a fine old man you are at disgraces, and what a bad old man you are at deeds! You have gathered baseness — may my Lord not give you life — and the gates of foolishness and error.)
and he said, satirizing his mother:
لحاك الله ثم لحاك أما ... ولقاك العقوق من البنينا
أغربالا إذا استودعت سرا ... وكانونا على المتحدثينا
(May Allah curse you, then curse you as a mother, and may He make you meet disobedience from sons. A sieve when entrusted with a secret, and a hearth upon those who speak!)
Among those who satirized his father was ʿAlī ibn Bassām. He said of his father:
هيك عمرت عمر عشرين نسرا ... أترى أنني أموت وتبقى؟
فلئن عشت بعد موتك يوما ... لأشقّنّ جيب مالك شقّا
(Such a one! You have lived the life of twenty vultures — do you think I will die and you will remain? If I live a day after your death, I will surely tear your wealth's pocket wide open.)
And he also said about him:
بنى أبو جعفر دارا فشيدها ... ومثله لخيار الدور بنّاء
فالجوع داخلها والذل خارجها ... وفي جوانبها بؤس وضراء
ما ينفع الدار من تشييد حائطها ... وليس داخلها خبز ولا ماء
(Abū Jaʿfar built a house and raised it high, and the like of him is a builder of the best houses. Hunger is inside it and humiliation outside it, and in its sides are misery and hardship. What good to a house is the raising of its wall, when inside it there is neither bread nor water?)
He lied: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr ibn Bassām was at the height of nobility, manliness and cleanliness; he was a man of luxury, with a fine mount and fine clothing, with an ambition for raising buildings. What Ibn al-Rūmī lamented him with indicates the falsehood of his son. Ibn al-Rūmī said of him:
أودى محمد بن نصر بعد ما ... ضربت به في جوده الأمثال
ملك تنافست العلا في عمره ... وتنافست في موته الآجال
من لم يعاين سير نعش محمد ... لم يدر كيف تسير الأجيال
وذخرته للدهر أعلم أنه ... كالحصن فيه لمن يئول مآل
وتمتعت نفسي بروح رجائه ... زمنا طويلا والتمتع مال
ورأيته كالشمس إن هي لم تنل ... فالرفق منها والضياء ينال
بالله أقسم ان عمرك ما انقضى ... حتى انقضى الإحسان والإجمال
(Muḥammad ibn Naṣr has perished, after proverbs were struck with him for his generosity. A king for whose life loftiness competed, and for whose death the terms of life competed. Whoever did not see the passage of Muḥammad's bier does not know how generations pass. I stored him up for Time, knowing that he was like a fortress for whoever seeks a refuge in it, and my soul enjoyed the breath of hoping for him for a long time, and enjoyment is wealth. I saw him like the sun: if one does not reach it, its gentleness and its light are still reached. By Allah I swear, your life did not end until beneficence and graciousness ended.)

dervis-irab:61-65.t:
* Vocabulary:
(لَأَحْتَنِكَنَّ): "I shall surely uproot his progeny by seduction", from احتنك الجراد الأرض (the locusts devoured the earth) when it stripped what was on it by eating; it is taken from al-ḥanak (the jaw/palate). From it comes what Sībawayh mentioned in their saying أحنك الشاتين, i.e. the one that eats most of the two sheep. It was also said that لأحتنكن means "I shall surely drive them and lead them wherever I wish", from حنك الدابة when the halter is put on its jaw. In al-Mukhtār: «حنك الفرس: he put the halter in its mouth (of the pattern نصر and ضرب), and likewise احتنكه; and احتنك الجراد الأرض: it ate what was on it and consumed its vegetation. And His words, the Exalted, relating from Iblīs: «لأحتنكن ذريته». Al-Farrāʾ said: "I shall surely gain mastery over them." And al-ḥanak is the beak; one says أسود مثل حنك الغراب ("black like the raven's beak") and أسود حانك like حالك ("pitch-black"); and al-ḥanak is what is beneath the chin of a human and others.» This root has branches that enumeration cannot encompass; in al-Qāmūs, Tāj al-ʿArūs and al-Lisān, the gist is as follows:
حنك يحنك and يحنك with ḍamma or kasra, ḥanakan: he grasped the thing and mastered it; and احتنك الفرس: he put the halter in its mouth; and حنك and حنّك: he chewed, then rubbed with the palate; and حنك يحنك and يحنك with ḍamma or kasra also, ḥanakan and ḥanakan, and حنّك, أحنك and احتنك الدهر الرجل: experiences, affairs and the vicissitudes of time made him wise, so he is ḥanīk; and تحنّك: he wound the turban beneath his chin; and احتنك also, the locusts devoured the earth, they ate what was on it; and احتنكه: he gained mastery over him; and استحنك: his eating became intense after being scant; and al-ḥanak, al-ḥunk and al-ḥinka: the noun from حنّكه الدهر; and al-ḥanak: the upper inside of the mouth, and the lower part from the front end of the two jawbones.
(وَاسْتَفْزِزْ): استفزه means he made him light (found him light). Al-fazz is the light one. In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj: «فزّ يفزّ فزّا: he was alone; فز عنه: he withdrew and turned aside; فزّ الظبي: the gazelle was startled; فزه: he disgraced him and overcame him, and made his heart fly, frightened him, disturbed him and removed him from his place; فز يفز فزيزا of a wound: it flowed with what was in it; فز فزازة and فزوزة: he was agitated and blazed; افتز عليه: he overcame; تفازّ الرجلان: the two men fought a duel; استفزه: he found him light, summoned him, made him agitated, disturbed him, drove him out of his house and killed him; al-fazz: the light man, and the calf of the wild cow; al-fazza: a leap in alarm.»
(وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ): shout at them and act upon them with all that you are able. In al-Mukhtār: «وجلب على فرسه يجلب جلبا (of the pattern طلب يطلب طلبا): he shouted at it from behind and urged it to race, and likewise أجلب عليه.» In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj:
جلبه يجلبه with ḍamma or kasra, jalban and jalaban (with sukūn or fatḥa): he drove it and brought it; جلب الرجل: the man was driven; جلب الجرح: the wound healed; أجلب القوم: he gathered them; جلبه and أجلبه: he threatened him secretly; جلب and أجلب for his family: he earned; جلب and أجلب على الفرس: he shouted at it and urged it to race; جلب and أجلب القوم: they clamoured and their voices mingled; al-jalaba: the mingling of voices and shouting; and al-jalab with two fatḥas: what is brought from one town to another, its plural being أجلاب. So what the common folk say about merchandise, "jalab" with two fatḥas, is correct and beyond reproach.
(وَرَجِلِكَ): with fatḥa then kasra, mounted and walking men. In al-Qāmūs: al-rajl: the راجل, one who walks on his feet; al-rājil: one who walks on his feet and does not ride, its plural رجل, رجّالة, رجّال, رجال, رجالى, رجالى and رجلان. One says: جاءت الخيالة والرجالة (the cavalry and infantry came), and أغار عليهم بخيله ورجله (he raided them with his horse and foot); and al-khayl are the cavalry. From it comes the hadith: "O horsemen of Allah, mount!"

* I'rab:
(وَإِذْ قُلْنا لِلْمَلائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ) The wāw is resumptive, and the adverbial is attached to an omitted element, i.e. "remember". The parsing of this verse, which is often repeated, has preceded. (قالَ: أَأَسْجُدُ لِمَنْ خَلَقْتَ طِيناً) The hamza is for rejecting interrogation, issuing from obstinacy, poor judgment, ignorance and stupidity. لمن: attached to أسجد. The clause خلقت is a ṣila. طينا is a ḥāl from the relative, the governor in it being أأسجد; or from the returning pronoun of this relative, i.e. "You created him of clay", the governor in it being خلقته. It is permissible for طينا to be a ḥāl even though it is inert (jāmid), because it indicates origin, as if he said "originating from clay". Some parsed it as accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "from clay", by the evidence of another verse in which the preposition is stated explicitly; he said «وخلقته من طين». Al-Zajjāj and others said it is a tamyīz, but that is remote. (قالَ أَرَأَيْتَكَ هذَا الَّذِي كَرَّمْتَ عَلَيَّ) The discussion of أرأيتك has been given in detail: it has the sense of "tell me", and the kāf is for emphasis of the address, with no grammatical position. هذا is the first object, and the relative is an adjective or badal of it; the second is omitted because the ṣila indicates it, i.e. "tell me about this one whom You have honoured above me by commanding me to prostrate to him: why did You honour him above me?" Allah the Exalted did not answer him on this question, out of belittling his affair and disdain for his standing, so the speech was abridged by omitting that; then He began with the oath, saying:
(لَئِنْ أَخَّرْتَنِ إِلى يَوْمِ الْقِيامَةِ لَأَحْتَنِكَنَّ ذُرِّيَّتَهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا) The lām prepares for the oath, and إن is conditional. أخرتني: verb, agent and direct object, the nūn being the protective nūn; it is the protasis. إلى يوم القيامة: attached to أخرتني. لأحتنكن: the lām occurs in the answer to the oath; أحتنكن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on the fatḥa because of its attachment to the heavy nūn of emphasis; the agent is latent, its implied form being "I". ذريته is the direct object. إلا is a particle of exception, and قليلا is the excepted from ذريته, accusative. The apodosis is omitted because the answer to the oath indicates it; further discussion of it will come in the section on rhetoric.
(قالَ اذْهَبْ فَمَنْ تَبِعَكَ مِنْهُمْ فَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ جَزاؤُكُمْ جَزاءً مَوْفُوراً) اذهب: imperative verb with a latent agent; the clause is the content of what is said. The "going" is not meant as the opposite of coming; rather its meaning is "go on to your business that you chose by your own pure will". It will come that He commanded him with four other things, so the total is five, all of them aimed at denouncing him, threatening him and luring him on. فمن: the fāʾ is resumptive, and من is conditional, a mubtadaʾ. تبعك: past verb, the agent latent, the kāf the direct object; it is in the position of the jussive as protasis. منهم is a ḥāl. فإن: the fāʾ links the apodosis; إن with its noun and khabar. جزاء is a mafʿūl muṭlaq of a verb indicated by جزاؤكم, i.e. "you will be recompensed with a recompense"; and I see no objection to its being a maṣdar made accusative by one like itself; more discussion of it will come in the section on benefits. It was said that it is a ḥāl muwaṭṭiʾa, and it was said that it is a tamyīz, and that is not remote. The discussion of this shift (iltifāt) will come in the section on rhetoric. موفورا is an adjective. (وَاسْتَفْزِزْ مَنِ اسْتَطَعْتَ مِنْهُمْ بِصَوْتِكَ وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ) واستفزز is a second command to Satan. من استطعت: من is a relative noun, the object of استفزز; the clause استطعت is a ṣila, and the object of استطعت is omitted, its implied form being "whom you are able to incite". منهم: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. بصوتك: attached to استفزز. أجلب is the third command. عليهم: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. بخيلك: attached to أجلب. ورجلك is conjoined to بخيلك, i.e. "rouse of them whom you can with your voice, and shout at them and drive them, accompanied by your horse and your foot". (وَشارِكْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْوالِ وَالْأَوْلادِ وَعِدْهُمْ وَما يَعِدُهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ إِلَّا غُرُوراً) وشاركهم is the fourth command; the hāʾ is the direct object. في الأموال: attached to شاركهم. The sharing in wealth means inciting them to amass it by forbidden, unlawful means such as usury and gambling and to spend it on forbidden things, depravity and disobedience. وعدهم is the fifth command; the hāʾ is the direct object; the promised thing is not mentioned for brevity, and what is meant is false and vain promises. وما: the wāw is circumstantial or parenthetical, and ما is negative. يعدهم الشيطان: imperfect verb, a fronted direct object and a postponed agent. In the speech there is an iltifāt, which will be discussed. إلا is a particle of restriction. غرورا may be an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "only a deceiving promise"; the attribution of deception to the maṣdar will come in the section on rhetoric. You may also parse it as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, i.e. "he promises them and fills them with false promises and honeyed wishes only for the sake of deception"; and the clause is circumstantial or parenthetical. (إِنَّ عِبادِي لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطانٌ وَكَفى بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلًا) The clause gives a reason for the command regarding the promise, i.e. "We command you this only because We know that you have no authority over Our righteous servants". إن and its noun; the clause ليس is its khabar. لك is the fronted khabar of ليس; عليهم is a ḥāl because it was originally an adjective of سلطان; and سلطان is the postponed noun of ليس. كفى: past verb; the bāʾ is redundant in the agent; and وكيلا is a tamyīz.

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain various arts, among them:
1- Mursal metaphor (al-majāz al-mursal) in using seeing in the sense of informing in His words «أرأيتك», because it is its cause, so the relationship in it is causality; the discussion of this has preceded.
2- Iltifāt from address to the third person. What the apparent sense required was to say: "and you promise them only deception", but he turned away from that to belittle his affair and to belittle the matter of the deception with which he promises them, on the one hand, and so that the speech would proceed in the manner of the third person, addressing all people, so that the ignorant may know and the falsifier be led back to the right.
3- Rational metaphor (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī) in attributing deception to the promise, in the way of the saying:
نهاره صائم وليله قائم
(His day is fasting and his night is standing in prayer.)
The details of this have preceded in their places.

* Benefits:
1- The governor of the mafʿūl muṭlaq:
The governor of the mafʿūl muṭlaq is either a maṣdar like it in wording and meaning, such as «فإن جهنم جزاؤكم جزاء موفورا», where جزاء is a mafʿūl muṭlaq and its governor is جزاؤكم, a maṣdar like it; or in meaning and not wording, as in أعجبني إيمانك تصديقا; or the verb derived from it, as in «وكلم الله موسى تكليما»; or from an adjective, namely an active participle, a passive participle, or the forms of intensity, but not the elative or the assimilated adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha). The active participle, as in «والصافات صفا»; the passive participle, as in الخبز مأكول أكلا; and the forms of intensity, as in زيد ضرّاب ضربا; but it is not permitted to say زيد حسن وجهه حسنا nor أقوم منك قياما. As for the poet's saying:
أما الملوك فأنت اليوم ألأمهم ... لؤما وأبيضهم سربال طباخ
(As for kings, today you are the basest of them in baseness, and the whitest of them in a cook's garment.)
لؤما is made accusative by an omitted verb. We return to the verse: some objected to the accusative of جزاء by the maṣdar, namely جزاؤكم, saying that although its wording is a maṣdar, its meaning is "that with which one is recompensed", since it is applied to Hell; so the meaning of the verse is that Hell is the thing with which you are recompensed. For the plausibility [Translator's note: the text reads «ولو جاهة», evidently «ولوجاهة»] of this objection, we say that it may be made accusative by an omitted verb indicated by جزاؤكم, the meaning being "you will be recompensed", or as a ḥāl muwaṭṭiʾa.

2- The ḥāl muwaṭṭiʾa:
The ḥāl muwaṭṭiʾa (with kasra on the ṭāʾ, or with fatḥa) is the inert, described ḥāl, because it is mentioned as a preparation for the qualification with a derived word or something like it, as in «فتمثل لها بشرا سويا»: بشرا is mentioned only as a preparation for mentioning سويا. The meaning of this is that when an inert noun is described by what may be a ḥāl, it is valid for it to be a ḥāl. Al-muwaṭṭiʾa in the language means "the one that prepares"; more of it will come in the discussion of this verse in Sūrat Maryam.

dervis-irab:66-69.t:
* Vocabulary:
(يُزْجِي): it makes run and move. In al-Qāmūs: «زجاه: he drove it and pushed it, like زجّاه and أزجاه», and from it comes the poet's saying:
يا أيها الراكب المزجي مطيته ... سائل بني أسد ما هذه الصوت
(O rider who drives his mount along, ask the Banū Asad: what is this sound?)
(حاصِباً): al-ḥāṣib is the wind that pelts (taḥṣibu), i.e. throws gravel; al-ḥaṣbāʾ is small stones, its singular being ḥaṣba like qaṣaba. In al-Miṣbāḥ: «وحصبته حصبا (of the pattern ضرب, and in one dialect of the pattern قتل): I pelted him with gravel.»
Abū ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybī said: al-ḥaṣb is throwing, i.e. a violent, pelting wind, which throws small pebbles. Al-Zajjāj said: al-ḥāṣib is dust containing gravel, so al-ḥāṣib is "possessing gravel", like lābin (possessing milk) and tāmir (possessing dates). The cloud that throws hail is also called ḥāṣib, and from it comes al-Farazdaq's saying:
مستقبلين جبال الشام تضربنا ... بحاصب كنديف القطن منثور
(Facing the mountains of Syria, which strike us with a pelting storm like carded cotton scattered.)
(قاصِفاً): al-qāṣif is the wind that has a qaṣīf, which is a violent sound, as if it were breaking (tataqaṣṣafu) apart. It was also said: the wind that passes over nothing without snapping it.
(تَبِيعاً): al-tabīʿ is the one who demands. Al-Shammākh said, describing an eagle:
تلوذ ثعالب الشرقين منها ... كما لاذ الغريم من التبيع
(The foxes of the two eastern lands take refuge from it, as the debtor takes refuge from the one who demands payment.)
That is: the foxes of al-Sharqayn, meaning the two east lands, flee from it as the debtor flees and takes shelter from the tabīʿ, i.e. the creditor who demands.

* I'rab:
(رَبُّكُمُ الَّذِي يُزْجِي لَكُمُ الْفُلْكَ فِي الْبَحْرِ لِتَبْتَغُوا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ) The clause gives a reason, to show His power, the Exalted. ربكم is the mubtadaʾ and الذي its khabar; the clause يزجي is a ṣila. لكم: attached to يزجي. الفلك: direct object. في البحر: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. لتبتغوا: the lām is for giving a reason; تبتغوا is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām of reason; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to تبتغوا, i.e. "that you may seek profit from His bounty". (إِنَّهُ كانَ بِكُمْ رَحِيماً) إن and its noun; the clause كان is its khabar; بكم: attached to رحيما; and رحيما is the khabar of kāna. (وَإِذا مَسَّكُمُ الضُّرُّ فِي الْبَحْرِ ضَلَّ مَنْ تَدْعُونَ إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ) The wāw is a conjunction, and إذا is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition. The clause مسكم is annexed to the adverb; the kāf is the direct object and الضر the agent. في البحر: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, i.e. "while you are at sea". The clause ضل has no position, because it is the answer to a non-jussive condition. من is the agent of ضل, and the clause تدعون is a ṣila. إلا إياه is an exception, i.e. "everyone you call upon departs from your thoughts except Him, for at that moment, at that very time, you remember Him"; it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) because it is included among those they mentioned. It is also possible that it be a disconnected one (munqaṭiʿ), i.e. "those you call upon of the gods fail to rescue you, but Allah alone, and He is the one whom you hope for alone". (فَلَمَّا نَجَّاكُمْ إِلَى الْبَرِّ أَعْرَضْتُمْ وَكانَ الْإِنْسانُ كَفُوراً) لما is a non-jussive conditional particle. نجاكم: past verb and direct object; it is the protasis, and its agent is "He". إلى البر: attached to نجاكم. أعرضتم is the apodosis. كان and its noun and khabar. (أَفَأَمِنْتُمْ أَنْ يَخْسِفَ بِكُمْ جانِبَ الْبَرِّ أَوْ يُرْسِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ حاصِباً) The hamza is for rejecting interrogation, and the fāʾ is a conjunction upon an omitted element, its implied form being "Have you been saved and so felt secure, and your being saved made you turn away?" أمنتم: verb and agent. أن يخسف: an interpreted maṣdar in the position of the accusative by removal of the preposition, "from His causing to sink"; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to أمنتم. بكم is a ḥāl, i.e. "accompanied by you", so the bāʾ is for accompaniment; it may also be attached to يخسف, in which case the bāʾ is causal. جانب البر is the object of يخسف. أو is a conjunction, and يرسل is conjoined to يخسف. عليكم: attached to يرسل. حاصبا: direct object. (ثُمَّ لا تَجِدُوا لَكُمْ وَكِيلًا) ثم is a conjunction of delay, and لا is negative. تجدوا is also conjoined to يرسل. لكم: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of وكيلا and was fronted before it. وكيلا is the direct object. (أَمْ أَمِنْتُمْ أَنْ يُعِيدَكُمْ فِيهِ تارَةً أُخْرى) أم is a conjunction, and it is the connected kind (muttaṣila), i.e. "which of the two matters is the case?". أمنتم: verb and agent. أن يعيدكم: an interpreted maṣdar in the position of the accusative by removal of the preposition; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to أمنتم. فيه: attached to يعيدكم. تارة is an adverbial also attached to يعيدكم, and أخرى is an adjective. (فَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ قاصِفاً مِنَ الرِّيحِ فَيُغْرِقَكُمْ بِما كَفَرْتُمْ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, and يرسل is conjoined to أن يعيدكم. عليكم: attached to يرسل. قاصفا: direct object. من الريح: an adjective. The fāʾ is a conjunction, and يغرقكم is conjoined to يرسل. بما: attached to يغرقكم, and ما is a maṣdar particle, i.e. "on account of your disbelief".
(ثُمَّ لا تَجِدُوا لَكُمْ عَلَيْنا بِهِ تَبِيعاً) ثم is a conjunction, and لا تجدوا is conjoined to يغرقكم. لكم: attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of تبيعا and was fronted before it, which is on the pattern of the saying of Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī:
لولا مفارقة الأحباب ما وجدت ... لها المنايا إلى أرواحنا سبلا
(Were it not for parting from loved ones, death would not have found paths to our souls.)
His saying لها is attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of سبلا; it is not permissible to attach it to وجدت, because وجد is not made transitive by the lām, but is transitive by itself.
علينا: attached to an omitted element, also a ḥāl; به is attached to تبيعا. It is possible that تبيعا contains the sense of "a helper", because the one who claims a right is the one who persists in demanding; in that case علينا is attached to it, i.e. "a helper against us".

dervis-irab:70-72.t:
* Vocabulary:
(فَتِيلًا): the discussion of al-naqīr and al-qiṭmīr has preceded. Al-fatīl is the thread lengthwise in the groove of the date stone; the husk is al-qiṭmīr; and the thread on its back is al-naqīr. So in the date stone there are three things: fatīl, qiṭmīr and naqīr. In al-Qāmūs: al-fatīl: the thread-like strip in the cleft of the date stone; al-qiṭmīr and al-qiṭmār (with kasra on the qāf in both): the thin husk between the stone and the fruit; and al-naqīr: the speck on the back of the stone.

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنا بَنِي آدَمَ وَحَمَلْناهُمْ فِي الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ) The wāw is resumptive, and the lām is the answer to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation. كرمنا: verb and agent. بني آدم: direct object. حملناهم is conjoined to كرمنا; it is a verb, agent and direct object. في البر والبحر: attached to حملناهم. (وَرَزَقْناهُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّباتِ وَفَضَّلْناهُمْ عَلى كَثِيرٍ مِمَّنْ خَلَقْنا تَفْضِيلًا)
ورزقناهم: verb, agent and also a direct object. من الطيبات: attached to رزقناهم. فضلناهم is also a conjoined clause. على كثير: attached to فضلناهم. ممن خلقنا is an adjective of كثير, and the clause خلقنا is a ṣila. تفضيلا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq. (يَوْمَ نَدْعُوا كُلَّ أُناسٍ بِإِمامِهِمْ) The adverbial is attached to an omitted element, its implied form being "remember". ندعو: imperfect verb, the agent latent, its implied form being "We". كل أناس: direct object. The clause ندعو is annexed to the adverbial. بإمامهم may be attached to ندعو, or attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl, i.e. "marked and known". What is meant by al-imām is the one whom they followed (i'tammū) in their worldly life, to whom they entrusted their affairs and the rulings of their livelihood, and whom they imitated in the matters of their world and their hereafter. (فَمَنْ أُوتِيَ كِتابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ فَأُولئِكَ يَقْرَؤُنَ كِتابَهُمْ وَلا يُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا) The fāʾ is a conjunction, and من is conditional or relative, in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ. أوتي: passive past verb, the deputy agent latent. كتابه is the second object. بيمينه: attached to أوتي. The fāʾ links the apodosis, and the clause أولئك is the apodosis or the khabar of the relative. أولئك is the mubtadaʾ, the clause يقرءون its khabar, and كتابهم the direct object. ولا: the wāw is a conjunction, and لا is negative. يظلمون: passive imperfect verb, the wāw a deputy agent. فتيلا stands in for a mafʿūl muṭlaq, i.e. "an injustice the size of a fatīl"; parallels of it have preceded. (وَمَنْ كانَ فِي هذِهِ أَعْمى) The wāw is a conjunction, and من is conditional or relative. كان: incomplete past verb. في هذه is the fronted khabar, the pointing referring to this world. أعمى is the postponed noun of kāna, and it is in the sense of an active participle. (فَهُوَ فِي الْآخِرَةِ أَعْمى وَأَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا) The fāʾ links the apodosis. هو is the mubtadaʾ, في الآخرة is a ḥāl, and أعمى is the khabar. It is either in the sense of an active participle like the first, i.e. "whoever in this world was blind to his proof, he is the same in the Hereafter"; or in the sense of the elative, which requires «min», and the meaning is "whoever in this world was blind, he is blind also in the Hereafter", what is meant being blindness of the heart that does not see guidance. وأضل is conjoined to أعمى, and سبيلا is a tamyīz.

dervis-irab:90-93.t:
* Vocabulary:
(يَنْبُوعاً): The yanbūʿ, with fatḥa on the yāʾ, is an abundant spring whose water does not run dry. It is of the pattern yafʿūl from nabaʿa l-māʾ, like yaʿbūb from ʿabba l-māʾ when it swells and its waves multiply. The nūn together with the bāʾ, as the fāʾ and ʿayn of the word, has a wonderful and regular secret: it indicates appearing and protruding. We have enumerated it in all its combinations and found that it never departs from conveying this meaning. Thus nabaʾa means "it rose"; al-nabaʾ is news; al-nubūʾa and al-nubuwwa are informing of the unseen or of the future; al-nābiʾ is the raised, humped place; and sayl nābiʾ is a flood that arrives suddenly, from where one does not know, and so is everything that appears. The poet said:
ألا فاسقياني وانفيا عنكما القذى ... وليس القذى بالعود يسقط في الخمر ولكن قذاها كل أشعث نابىء ... أتتنا به الأقدار من حيث لا ندري
(Come, give me drink and keep the mote away from yourselves; the mote is not a twig that falls into the wine, but its mote is every dishevelled intruder that fate brought us from where we knew not.)
Nabba l-tays nabban means the billy goat bleated when in rut, and nothing is more evident than that. A rumḥ muṭṭarid al-anābīb is a spear with regular joints; one drank from the unbūb (spout) of the jug; and "he has an unbūb of palm and other plants". The poet said:
أو من مشعشعة ورهاء نشوتها ... أو من أنابيب رمّان وتفّاح
(Or from a diluted, foolish wine, its intoxication, or from the tubes [stems] of pomegranate and apple.)
Nabata l-makān means the place came to have visible vegetation; al-nabt and al-nabāt appeared in the earth; al-nābita, feminine of al-nābit, is the rising generation of children and cattle. Nabatha l-turāb means he extracted the soil from the pit; nabathū ʿan al-amr means they investigated it, and they continue to nabathū each other about secrets and to investigate reports. Al-unbūtha, with ḍamma on the hamza, is a children's game in which they bury something in a small hole, and whoever extracts it wins. "He is nafffāj nabbāj" means he has nothing but talk. Nabaḥathu l-kilāb means the dogs barked at him, a well-known usage, and istanbaḥa l-ḍayf l-kilāb means the guest, on appearing, made the dogs bark. Al-Akhṭal said, in what is the most scathing verse of satire:
قوم إذا استنبح الأضياف كلبهم ... قالوا لأمهم: بولي على النار
(A people whose dog, when guests make it bark, they tell its mother: "Piss on the fire [to put it out, so guests will not find them]".)
Nabadha l-shayʾ min yadihi means he threw it away and cast it; ṣabī manbūdh is a foundling; "so-and-so picked up a foundling"; nabadha amrī warāʾa ẓahrihi means he cast my command behind his back; nabadha l-nabīdh means to put dates in a jar or another vessel; al-nabīdh is the soaked date and also the wine pressed from grapes and other fruits, its plural being anbidha, and al-nabbādh is the seller of nabīdh. Nabara l-ghulām means the boy grew robust; nabara l-mughannī means the singer raised his voice after lowering it; nabara l-ḥarf means he pronounced it with a hamza; al-minbar is a raised place which the preacher or admonisher ascends to speak to the crowd from it, so called for its height, with the mīm given kasra by analogy with instruments, and the plural is manābir. Al-nabz is a nickname, and nabazahu bi-kadhā means he nicknamed him that he might be known by it, which is common for ugly nicknames. Nabasa bi-l-majlis and nabbasa mean he spoke, and it is mostly used after a negative: "he did not utter a word"; you say "I spoke to him and he frowned and uttered nothing". Nabasha l-shayʾ l-mastūr means he brought out and revealed the concealed thing; nabasha l-kanz min al-arḍ means he uncovered and extracted the treasure from the earth; and "he digs up secrets". The poet said:
مهلا بني عمنا مهلا موالينا ... لا تنبشوا بيننا ما كان مدفونا
(Gently, sons of our uncle, gently, our kinsmen; do not dig up between us what was buried.)
He "digs for his dependants and scratches" when he extracts their sustenance from here and there and uses stratagems. Intabasha l-ʿurūq min al-arḍ means he dug out the roots from the earth. Al-Kumayt said:
موتهنّ انتباشهن من الأر ... ض ويحيين ما سكنّ القبورا
(Their death is their being dug out of the earth, and they live while they dwell in the graves.)
That is, so long as the roots are under the ground they are alive, but when dug out they die. Al-nabbāsh, of the intensive pattern faʿʿāl, is the one who digs up graves. Nabaṣa l-ghulām bi-l-ṭāʾir wa-l-kalb means the boy pressed his lips together and called it. Nabaḍa ʿirquhu nabḍan wa-nabaḍānan means his vein throbbed, and you say: "I saw a flash of lightning like the throb of a vein." Nabaṭa l-māʾ means the water gushed; istanbaṭa l-biʾr means he brought out its water; and istanbaṭa l-ʿarab means the Arabs became Nabateans. Khālid ibn al-Walīd said to ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn Buqayla: "Are you Arabs or Nabateans?" He said: "Arabs who became Nabateans, and Nabateans who became Arabs." And Abū l-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī said:
أين امرؤ القيس والعذارى ... إذ مال من تحته الغبيط
استنبط العرب في الموامي ... بعدك واستعرب النبيط
(Where is Imruʾ al-Qays, and the maidens, when the saddle-frame tilted beneath him? After you the Arabs dug wells in the wastelands, and the Nabateans turned Arab.)
What was said about al-nabʿ and al-yanbūʿ has already been mentioned. Nabagha l-shayʾ means it came out and appeared; nabagha l-rajul means the man composed poetry and excelled in it. It is said that al-Nābigha composed poetry when he was old and excelled, so he was called al-Nābigha; others say it was for his saying:
وحلت في بني القين بن جسر ... فقد نبغت لنا منهم شئون
(She settled among the Banū l-Qayn ibn Jasr, and affairs from them have arisen for us.)
He is a nābigha (prodigy) among the prodigies, and nabagha in knowledge and in every craft. Nabaqa l-shayʾ yanbuqu means it appeared; and al-nabiq, al-nabq, al-nubq and al-nabaq are the fruit of the lote tree, the singular being nabaqa. One of the Arabs said: "The nabiq pleases me, and the nabq harms me." In the hadith: «ونبقها كقلال هجر» ("and its fruits are like the jars of Hajar"). Waqaʿnā fī nabk min al-arḍ wa-nibāk, plural of nabka, means we came to a knoll with a pointed head; nabaka l-makān means the place was raised; and hiḍāb nawābik are rising hills. Dhū l-Rumma said:
طواهن تغويري إذا الآل أرفلت ... به الشمس أزر الحزورات النوابك
(My travelling at noon folded them up, when the mirage let the sun trail its robes over the rising hillocks.)
Nabula l-rajul means the man had manifest nobility and excellence; a rajul nābil and nabbāl is one who has arrows (nabl). Imruʾ al-Qays said:
أيقتلني والمشرفيّ مضاجعي ... ومسنونة زرق كأنياب أغوال
وليس بذي رمح فيطعنني به ... وليس بذي سيف وليس بنبّال
(Will he kill me while the Mashrafī sword is my bedfellow and sharpened blue-bright arrowheads like the fangs of ghouls? He has no spear to stab me with, nor a sword, nor is he an archer.)
A rajul tinbāl is a short man. Nabaha yantabihu lil-amr means he grasped it and was a man of eminence and honour. Nabā l-sayf ʿani l-ḍarība nabwan wa-nabwa means the sword glanced off the thing struck; sayf nābin; and every sharp blade has its glance-off. The poet said:
أنا السيف إلا أن للسيف نبوة ... ومثلي لا تنبو عليك مضاربه
(I am the sword, except that a sword may glance off; but one like me has edges that never glance off against you.)
Ḥāfiẓ Ibrāhīm eyed the sky of this meaning and said:
لا تلم كفي إذا السيف نبا ... صّح مني العزم والدهر أبى
(Do not blame my hand if the sword glanced off; my resolve was sound, and it was Fate that refused.)
[Translator's note: the second hemistich is printed in the source as «صّح مني العزم والدهر أبى»; it appears to read «صَحَّ مني العزم»; translated as such.]
(كِسَفاً): Pieces. One says kasaftu l-thawb, meaning I cut the cloth. Al-Zajjāj said that kasafa l-shayʾ means he covered it; it is said that this is not known from anyone else. In al-Asās: "This is a kisfa, a kisaf and a kasf of clouds; and give me a kisfa of the cloth: a piece."
(قَبِيلًا): A guarantor of what you say, a witness to its soundness. It is also said to mean face to face and in plain sight. It is also said to be the plural of qabīla, meaning with the classes of angels, tribe by tribe, bearing witness to the soundness of what you say. The language admits all of these.
(زُخْرُفٍ): Gold, which is what is meant here. It has various meanings, among them the beauty of a thing; the zukhruf of speech is its deceptively gilded falsehoods; the zukhruf of the earth is the colours of its plants, the plural being zakhārif; zakhrafa l-shayʾ means he beautified and adorned it; and zakhrafa l-kalām means he gilded it with lies.

* I'rab:
(وَقالُوا: لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّى تَفْجُرَ لَنا مِنَ الْأَرْضِ يَنْبُوعاً) The wāw is a conjunction; (قالوا) is a verb and an agent; (لن) is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; (نؤمن) is put in the accusative by it, and the agent of (نؤمن) is latent, its implied form being "we"; (لك) is attached to (نؤمن); (حتى) is a particle of limit and genitive; (تفجر) is an imperfect verb put in the accusative by an implied (أن) after (حتى); (لنا) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted ḥāl; (من الأرض) is attached to (تفجر); and (ينبوعا) is a direct object.
(أَوْ تَكُونَ لَكَ جَنَّةٌ مِنْ نَخِيلٍ وَعِنَبٍ فَتُفَجِّرَ الْأَنْهارَ خِلالَها تَفْجِيراً) (أو) is a conjunction; (تكون) is conjoined to (تفجر), and this is the second of their six demands. (لك) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted khabar of (تكون), put first; (جنة) is its postponed name. (فتفجر): the fāʾ is a conjunction and (تفجر) is conjoined to (تكون); its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; (الأنهار) is a direct object; (خلالها) is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl, that is "being in its midst"; and (تفجيرا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(أَوْ تُسْقِطَ السَّماءَ كَما زَعَمْتَ عَلَيْنا كِسَفاً) (أو) is a conjunction; (تسقط) is conjoined to what preceded, and this is the third demand. (السماء) is a direct object. The kāf is a preposition or a noun meaning "like", and together with the maṣdar (ما) interpreted as a maṣdar it is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar or accusative as a ḥāl. (علينا) is attached to (تسقط), and (كسفا) is a ḥāl from (السماء). The allusion is to His saying, the Exalted: «إن نشأ نخسف بهم الأرض أو نسقط عليهم كسفا من السماء».
(أَوْ تَأْتِيَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْمَلائِكَةِ قَبِيلًا) This is the fourth of their obstinate demands. (بالله) is attached to (تأتي); (الملائكة) is conjoined to (الله); and (قبيلا) is a ḥāl from (الله) and (الملائكة). Its meaning was given earlier in the section on Vocabulary.
(أَوْ يَكُونَ لَكَ بَيْتٌ مِنْ زُخْرُفٍ أَوْ تَرْقى فِي السَّماءِ) These are the fifth and sixth demands. (لك) is the preposed khabar of (يكون), (بيت) is the postponed name of (يكون), and (من زخرف) is attached to an omitted adjective of (بيت). (أو) is a conjunction and (ترقى) is conjoined to what precedes; with it the six obstinate demands are completed. (في السماء) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (ترقى), and the meaning of ascent is going up into the sky.
(وَلَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لِرُقِيِّكَ حَتَّى تُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْنا كِتاباً نَقْرَؤُهُ) The wāw is a conjunction; (لن) is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; (نؤمن) is put in the accusative by it and its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "we"; (لرقيك) is attached to (نؤمن); (حتى) is a particle of limit and genitive; (تنزل) is an imperfect verb put in the accusative by an implied (أن), and its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; (علينا) is attached to (تنزل); (كتابا) is a direct object; and the clause (نقرؤه) is an adjective of (كتابا) or an anticipated ḥāl from the (نا) in (علينا).
(قُلْ سُبْحانَ رَبِّي هَلْ كُنْتُ إِلَّا بَشَراً رَسُولًا) (قل) is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you", that is: say in reply to obstinacy and contention. (سبحان ربي) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, and the clause is the content of the saying. Its meaning is wonder at this contentiousness and glorification of Allah, Glory be to Him, above anyone sharing in His power. (هل) is a particle of interrogation whose meaning is negation and denial; (كنت) is a defective past verb and the tāʾ is its name; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (بشرا) is the khabar of (كنت) or a ḥāl; and (رسولا) is an adjective or the khabar of (كنت).

dervis-irab:32-39.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الزِّنى): It is written with yāʾ because it is the maṣdar of zanā yazni, and it is written with alif on the view that it is a shortened form of al-zināʾ with madd. They say "he is a zānin," between al-zinā and al-zināʾ, with shortening and lengthening. Al-Farazdaq said:
أبا خالد من يزن يعلم زناؤه ... ومن يشرب الخرطوم يصبح مسكّرا
(O Abū Khālid, whoever commits fornication, his fornication becomes known; and whoever drinks the khurṭūm [wine] wakes up intoxicated.)
Al-Farrāʾ said: the shortened form is from zanā, and the lengthened from zānā; it is said zānāhā muzānāt^an wa-zināʾ^an; "so-and-so went out to commit fornication and to transgress"; "she was fornicated with"; "he is a child of fornication (zinya)"; and "he is a zinya," with fatḥa and with kasra.
(القسطاس): It is Greek, arabized, as has preceded, and we mentioned before that this does not impair the Arabic character of the Qur'an, because when the Arabs use a foreign word and treat it like their own speech in declension, definiteness, indefiniteness and the like, it becomes Arabic; more of this useful discussion will come. Al-qisṭās is with ḍamma and with kasra, and it is al-qarasṭūn, that is, the steelyard (qabbān); and it was said that it is any balance, small or large.
(وَلا تَقْفُ): "Do not follow." It is said qafā atharahu and qāfahu. It was said that it is taken from al-qafā (the nape), as though he follows matters from behind, following and pursuing them. And it was said that al-qafw resembles slander (ʿaḍīha), and from it the ḥadīth: "Whoever accuses (qafā) a believer of what is not in him, Allah will confine him in the mire of ruin (radghat al-khabāl) until he comes out of it." And they recited for one of them:
ومثل الدمى شم العرانين ساكن ... بهن الحياء لا يشعن التقافيا
(Like statues, high-nosed, modesty dwells in them; they do not spread mutual accusation.)
He describes women as beautiful like statues and likens them to houses, and likens modesty to a people who dwell in them, by way of the makniyya metaphor, dwelling being the imaginative element of that. He says they do not "spread," that is, do not show, al-taqāfī, that is, mutual following by slander, from qafawtuhu when you follow him with backbiting.
Al-Kumayt said:
ولا أرمي البريء بغير ذنب ... ولا أقفو الحواصن إن قفينا
(I do not charge the innocent without a fault, nor do I accuse chaste women even if we are accused.)
He says: I do not accuse the innocent of something false, but of a verified fault, and I do not follow chaste women speaking of them obscenely as long as they remain chaste, if people follow them and speak of them; so how, if no one speaks of them?

* I'rab:
(وَلا تَقْرَبُوا الزِّنى إِنَّهُ كانَ فاحِشَةً وَساءَ سَبِيلًا): The wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تقربوا is an imperfect verb jussive by لا, the wāw being the agent; الزنا is the direct object; the clause إنه is explanatory of cause and has no grammatical position; inna and its noun, and the clause كان is its predicate; the noun of كان is latent, its implied form being "he"; فاحشة is its predicate; ساء is a past verb of blame, the agent being latent; سبيلا is a tamyīz (specification); and the specified object of blame is omitted, that is, "it."
(وَلا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ): ولا تقتلوا is conjoined to what precedes; النفس is the direct object; التي is an adjective and the clause حرم الله is the ṣila; إلا is a particle of restriction; and بالحق is attached to تقتلوا, the bāʾ being causal, or attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from the agent of تقتلوا, in which case it is of accompaniment, that is, "accompanied by right."
(وَمَنْ قُتِلَ مَظْلُوماً فَقَدْ جَعَلْنا لِوَلِيِّهِ سُلْطاناً): The wāw is resumptive; من is conditional and a mubtadaʾ; قتل is a passive past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis; the deputy agent (nāʾib fāʾil) is latent, its implied form being "he"; مظلوما is a ḥāl. فقد: the fāʾ connects the apodosis, and قد is a particle of certainty; جعلنا is a verb and agent; لوليه is the second object of جعلنا and سلطانا is the first object of جعلنا, that is, a proof by which he prevails over him.
(فَلا يُسْرِفْ فِي الْقَتْلِ إِنَّهُ كانَ مَنْصُوراً): The fāʾ is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; يسرف is an imperfect verb jussive by لا, and its agent is latent, referring to the guardian (walī), that is, "let him not kill other than the killer, nor two when the killer is one," as is the custom of the Jāhiliyya, according to the saying of Muhalhil ibn Rabīʿa:
كل قتيل في كليب غره ... حتى ينال القتل آل مرة
(Every slain man in the matter of Kulayb is a trifle, until killing reaches the family of Murra.)
وفي القتل is attached to يسرف; the clause إنه is explanatory of cause; inna and its noun, and the clause كان is the predicate of inna; the noun of كان is latent; and منصورا is its predicate.
(وَلا تَقْرَبُوا مالَ الْيَتِيمِ إِلَّا بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ): ولا تقربوا is also a conjunction; مال اليتيم is the direct object; إلا is a particle of restriction; and بالتي is an exception made complete from the most general of states (istithnāʾ mufarragh min aʿamm al-aḥwāl), that is, "do not approach it in any circumstance except with the quality or method that is best," namely guarding it, preserving it and investing it for the benefit of the orphan; هي is the mubtadaʾ and أحسن the khabar, and the clause has no position because it is the ṣila of the relative noun.
(حَتَّى يَبْلُغَ أَشُدَّهُ): حتى is a particle of limit and a preposition; يبلغ is subjunctive by an implied أن after حتى; and what is meant by al-ashudd is his reaching a rank at which he handles things well. The meaning of al-ashudd has preceded: that it is a singular meaning strength, or a plural with no singular from its own word; and it was said that it is the plural of shidda or shadd. In the book Maʿānī al-Qurʾān by al-Farrāʾ: forty is closer to the correct.
(وَأَوْفُوا بِالْعَهْدِ إِنَّ الْعَهْدَ كانَ مَسْؤُلًا): أوفوا is an imperative verb and the wāw is the agent; بالعهد is attached to أوفوا; inna and its noun, and the clause كان is its predicate; and مسئولا is the predicate of كان. The meaning of "mas'ūlan" is "demanded," as though the one who made the covenant is asked to fulfil it, and the preposition and its genitive noun were omitted for lightness, that is, "about it"; it has been mentioned in the rest of the verses, as will come; and another view is permissible, which will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(وَأَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ إِذا كِلْتُمْ وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ): وأوفوا is an imperative verb and the wāw is the agent; الكيل is the object of أوفوا; إذا is a future adverbial that includes the meaning of a condition, and the clause كلتم is annexed to the adverbial; its apodosis is omitted, indicated by His saying أوفوا الكيل. وزنوا بالقسطاس المستقيم is conjoined to أوفوا الكيل.
(ذلِكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا): ذلك is the mubtadaʾ and خير the khabar; أحسن is conjoined to خير; and تأويلا is a tamyīz, that is, "better in outcome"; taʾwīl is a comparative-intensive form from āla when it returns, and it is what it returns to in the Hereafter.
(وَلا تَقْفُ ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ): لا is prohibitive; تقف is jussive by لا, the sign of its jussive being the omission of the weak letter, namely the wāw; its agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; ما is the direct object; the clause ليس is the ṣila; ولك is the fronted predicate of ليس; وبه is attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl; and it is not permissible to attach it to علم, because the object of a maṣdar does not precede it. Some said it is attached to what لك is attached to, namely "being established," but that is remote. The meaning of the verse is a prohibition against a person saying what he does not know or acting upon what he has no knowledge of; a group of exegetes made it specific to certain matters, but its generality is preferable. And علم is the postponed noun of ليس.
(إِنَّ السَّمْعَ وَالْبَصَرَ وَالْفُؤادَ كُلُّ أُولئِكَ كانَ عَنْهُ مَسْؤُلًا): inna and its noun; والبصر والفؤاد are conjoined to السمع; كل is the mubtadaʾ, أولئك its muḍāf ilayhi, and the clause كان is the khabar; عنه is attached to مسئولا; and مسئولا is the predicate of كان. More detail on this verse will come in the sections on Rhetoric and Benefits.
(وَلا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحاً): لا is prohibitive; تمش is jussive by it, and its agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; في الأرض is attached to تمش; and مرحا is a ḥāl on the estimate of an omitted muḍāf, that is, "possessing exuberance," that is, "do not walk on the earth as one possessing exuberance, that is, exulting, marked by pride and conceit." Al-Akhfash did well in preferring the maṣdar over the active participle, as if it were the very exuberance; and it is permissible to parse it as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, as Abū l-Baqāʾ said.
(إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَخْرِقَ الْأَرْضَ وَلَنْ تَبْلُغَ الْجِبالَ طُولًا): The clause is explanatory of cause and has no position, as though it explained the reason for the prohibition, that is, "you will not make splits and holes in it by your treading on it"; inna and its noun, and the clause لن تخرق الأرض is its predicate; ولن تبلغ الجبال is conjoined to لن تخرق; and طولا is a tamyīz converted from the agent, that is, "and your height will not reach the mountains"; and it was said to be a maṣdar in the position of ḥāl or a mafʿūl lahu. More discussion will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(كُلُّ ذلِكَ كانَ سَيِّئُهُ عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ مَكْرُوهاً): كل is the mubtadaʾ and ذلك its muḍāf ilayhi; the demonstrative refers to the twenty-five qualities mentioned above, beginning from His saying لا تجعل مع الله إلها آخر, and the detail of counting them will come in the section on Benefits; كان is a defective past verb; سيئه is its noun; عند ربك is an adverbial attached to مكروها; and مكروها is the predicate of كان.
(ذلِكَ مِمَّا أَوْحى إِلَيْكَ رَبُّكَ مِنَ الْحِكْمَةِ): ذلك is the mubtadaʾ, that is, the qualities that preceded; مما is the khabar and the clause أوحى is the ṣila; إليك is attached to أوحى; ربك is the agent; and من الحكمة is a ḥāl from the omitted returning pronoun of the relative, that is, "from that which He revealed to you, while it is part of wisdom, which is the knowledge of truth for its own sake and of the good in order to act on it," or a ḥāl from the relative itself. These qualities were begun and concluded with the prohibition of polytheism.
(وَلا تَجْعَلْ مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلهاً آخَرَ فَتُلْقى فِي جَهَنَّمَ مَلُوماً مَدْحُوراً): ولا تجعل is conjoined to what precedes; مع is an adverb of place attached to an omitted element which is the second object of تجعل; إلها is the first object; آخر is an adjective; فتلقى: the fāʾ is the fāʾ of causation; the deputy agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; في جهنم is attached to تلقى; and ملوما ومدحورا are two ḥāl.

* Rhetoric:
This verse comprises many arts of rhetoric, which we set down as follows.

1- Iṭnāb (elaboration):
In the words of Him the Exalted: «ومن قتل مظلوما فقد جعلنا لوليه سلطانا فلا يسرف في القتل إنه كان منصورا». The meaning of this verse came concisely in the words of Him the Exalted «ولكم في القصاص حياة», but the first is iṭnāb and the second is concision (ījāz), and both are described as equivalence (musāwāt). We have spoken about concision; let us now speak about iṭnāb and equivalence. Iṭnāb is taken originally from aṭnaba fī l-shayʾ when he exaggerates in it; it is said aṭnabat al-rīḥ when the wind becomes intense in its blowing, and aṭnaba fī l-sayr when he intensifies his travel. In the terminology of the rhetoricians it is the increase of the wording over the meaning for a benefit. If there is no benefit in the increase, it is called tatwīl (prolixity) if the increase is not determinate, and ḥashw (padding) if it is determinate. Tatwīl is like the saying of ʿAntara ibn Shaddād:
حييت من طلل تقادم عهده ... أقوى وأقفر بعد أم الهيثم
(Greetings to you, O ruin whose time is old, which became empty and desolate after Umm al-Haytham.)
and ḥashw is like the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā:
وأعلم علم اليوم والأمس قبله ... ولكنني عن علم ما في غد عم
(I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but of the knowledge of what is in tomorrow I am blind.)
Iṭnāb occurs in several ways, which we summarize as follows.
a- Emphasis and affirmation (al-taʾkīd wa-l-taqrīr), which is both literal and figurative. The literal is like their saying "I saw him with my eye," "I seized it with my hand," "I trod on it with my foot," and "I tasted it with my mouth." All of this a supposer may think unnecessary, for seeing is only with the eye, seizing only with the hand, treading only with the foot, and tasting only with the mouth; but the matter is not as he imagines; rather it applies to everything that is hard to attain and great to reach. Among its splendid examples in poetry is the saying of al-Buḥturī:
تأمل من خلال السجف وانظر ... بعينك ما شربت ومن سقاني
تجد شمس الضحى تدنو بشمس ... إليّ من الرحيق الخسرواني
(Look through the gaps in the curtain and see with your own eye what I drank and who served me. You will find the sun of the forenoon bringing me a sun of Khusrawānī wine.)
Since attending this gathering is among what is rare to find and attain, and the cupbearer was of such beauty, he said "see with your eye." In this vein much of it occurs in the Noble Qur'an; Allah the Exalted said: «ذلك قولكم بأفواهكم». And the figurative is like the words of Him the Exalted: «فإنها لا تعمى الأبصار ولكن تعمى القلوب التي في الصدور». The benefit of mentioning the breasts here is that it is customarily known that blindness in reality has its place in sight, which is when the pupil is struck by something that obliterates its light, and its use for the heart is a simile and likeness. So when it was intended to establish what is contrary to the customary and known, ascribing blindness to hearts, the matter needed additional depiction and definition in order to affirm that the place of blindness is the hearts, not the breasts.
b- Mention of the particular after the general: like the words of Him the Exalted «تنزل الملائكة والروح فيها». Allah the Exalted singled out al-Rūḥ, who is Jibrīl, for mention, though he is included in the generality of the angels, in honour of him and exaltation of his standing, as though he were of another kind. So the benefit of the addition here is special acclaim.
c- Mention of the general after the particular: like the words of Him the Exalted: «ربي اغفر لي ولوالديّ ولمن دخل بيتي مؤمنا وللمؤمنين والمؤمنات». Allah the Exalted mentioned the believing men and believing women, two general words in whose generality those mentioned before are included; the purpose of this addition is to convey inclusiveness together with care for the particular, mentioned once alone and once included under the general.
d- Clarification after vagueness: like the words of Him the Exalted: «وقضينا إليه ذلك الأمر أن دابر هؤلاء مقطوع مصبحين». His saying ذلك الأمر is vague, and his saying أن دابر هؤلاء مقطوع مصبحين is a clarification of the vagueness contained in the word al-amr, for further establishing the meaning in the hearer's mind, once in a general and vague manner and once in a detailed and clarified manner.
e- Repetition to establish the meaning: this is a subject with many branches and numerous routes, which would need volumes to enumerate, but we mention what serves as an indicator and guide to the rest, like the saying of ʿAntara ibn Shaddād in some transmissions of his muʿallaqa:
يدعون عنتر والسيوف كأنها ... لمع البوارق في سحاب مظلم
يدعون عنتر والرماح كأنها ... أشطان بئر في لبان الأدهم
(They call "ʿAntar!" while the swords are like the flashes of lightning in a dark cloud; they call "ʿAntar!" while the spears are like the ropes of a well in the chest of the black horse.)
The repetition in the two verses of ʿAntara establishes the meaning in the hearer's soul and entrenches it in his mind, and here it is for the sake of boasting; it holds throughout oratory and in places of boasting, praise, guidance and warning. It may be for lamentation, like the saying of al-Ḥusayn ibn Muṭayr, lamenting Maʿn ibn Zāʾida:
فيا قبر معن أنت أول حفرة ... من الأرض خطّت للسماحة موضعا
ويا قبر معن كيف واريت جوده ... وقد كان منه البر والبحر مرتعا
(O grave of Maʿn, you are the first pit of the earth marked out as a place for generosity! O grave of Maʿn, how did you cover his generosity, when land and sea had been his pasture?)
Among them is the lengthening of the separation, like the saying of the poet:
لقد علم الحيّ اليمانون أنني ... إذا قلت أما بعد اني خطيبها
(The Yemeni tribes have known that when I say "Now then," I am their orator.)
And the parenthesis (al-iʿtirāḍ): it is that a clause or more, with no grammatical position, is brought in the course of speech or between two speeches connected in meaning, for a purpose the eloquent speaker intends; it was mentioned before. Among it is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī:
ألا زعمت بنو سعد بأني- ألا كذبوا- كبير السن فان
(Lo! The Banū Saʿd claimed that I — lo, they lied! — am old and frail.)
The clause "ألا كذبوا" came as a parenthesis between the noun of inna and its predicate, to hasten to draw attention to the falsehood of whoever accused him of old age.
z- Tadhyīl (appending): it is following clauses with another clause that contains their meaning, as emphasis of them, like the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:
تزور فتى يعطي على الحمد ماله ... ومن يعط أثمان المحامد يحمد
(You visit a young man who gives his wealth for praise; and whoever gives the prices of praises is praised.)
The meaning was complete in the first hemistich, then it was appended with the second hemistich for emphasis.
ḥ- Iḥtirās (precaution): its discussion has preceded, and among it is the saying of Ibn al-Muʿtazz:
صببنا عليها ظالمين سياطنا ... فطارت بها أيد سراع وأرجل
(We poured our whips upon her, being unjust, and swift hands and legs flew with her.)
Had we dropped the word "ظالمين," the hearer would suppose that Ibn al-Muʿtazz's horse was dull and deserved the beating, which is contrary to the intention.
More examples of iṭnāb will come in their places in this book.
As for equivalence (musāwāt), it is that the meanings be equal to the words and the words equal to the meanings, neither exceeding the other nor falling short of it. An example of it has preceded in the words of Him the Exalted: «إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان» etc. Among its examples in poetry is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:
فانك كالليل الذي هو مدركي ... وان خلت أن المنتأى عنك واسع
(You are like the night, which will overtake me, though I imagined the place of withdrawal from you was wide.)
and the saying of Ṭarafa:
ستبدي لك الأيام ما كنت جاهلا ... ويأتيك بالأخبار من لم تزود
(The days will show you what you did not know, and he whom you did not provision will bring you the news.)
The Qur'an is full of examples of equivalence, and they will come in their places, if Allah wills.

2- Metaphor:
In the words of Him the Exalted: «إن العهد كان مسئولا». We have already presented that it proceeds on the literal sense with the omission of the preposition and its genitive noun; it is also possible that the speech proceeds by way of the makniyya metaphor, by likening the covenant to one who breaks his covenant, and attributing questioning to it is imaginative (takhyīl).

3- Sarcasm (al-tahakkum):
It has been mentioned before, because the walk of exuberance comprises heaviness of tread and boasting over the earth by walking on it and lording over others, even if the proud person is light of weight, ugly of look and thin of build, according to the saying of al-Mutanabbī:
أفي كل يوم تحت ضبني شويعر ... ضعيف يقاويني قصير يطاول
(Is it every day that under my gathering there is a petty poet, weak, who contends with me, short, who tries to be tall over me?)

* Benefits:
In these comprehensive verses there are many benefits; we will take up the important among them, following our method in this book. Among them is the attachment of the preposition and its genitive noun in the words of Him the Exalted:
«كل أولئك كان عنه مسئولا». In the section on I'rab we attached it to مسئولا and made the deputy agent a pronoun referring to كل, that is, "each one of them was questioned about itself," meaning about what its owner did with it. Al-Zamakhsharī attributed مسئولا to the preposition and its genitive noun and made it the equivalent of the deputy agent. This is an oversight on the part of al-Zamakhsharī, which is beneath him, because the preposition and its genitive noun are put in the place of the agent or its deputy only if the verb or what stands for it comes first; if it comes later, that is not valid, because a noun when it precedes the verb becomes a mubtadaʾ, and a preposition, when it is obligatory, cannot be a mubtadaʾ. So «عنه» is not the deputy of the agent, contrary to the author of al-Kashshāf, nor the pronoun of the maṣdar as some said; rather the deputy in this verse is a pronoun referring to what the noun of كان refers to, namely the one charged with obligations (al-mukallaf), indicated by the meaning, the estimate being "mas'ūlan huwa," that is, the mukallaf. The pronoun of كان was not implied as referring to كل only so that مسئولا would not be devoid of a pronoun and thus be attributed to عنه, and that is not permissible.
The words of Ibn Hishām: "And the saying of some regarding the words of Him the Exalted: «إن السمع والبصر والفؤاد كل أولئك كان عنه مسئولا» that عنه is nominative in position by مسئولا; the correct view is that the noun of كان is the pronoun of the mukallaf, even though no mention of him is found, and that the one made nominative by مسئولا is a latent pronoun in it referring to him also, and that عنه is in the position of accusative," that is, as a second object of مسئولا, because it takes two objects, the second with ʿan.

The twenty-five qualities:
We promised you the counting of the twenty-five qualities to which reference was made by His saying «كل ذلك», and this is their counting in order:
1- Do not set up with Allah another god.
2 and 3- His saying "Your Lord has decreed…" to the end of the verse, because it contains two obligations, namely the worship of Allah and the prohibition of worshipping other than Him.
4- And kindness to parents.
5- So do not say to them "uff."
6- And do not rebuke them.
7- And say to them a generous word.
8- And lower to them the wing of humility.
9- And say "My Lord, have mercy on them."
10- And give the relative his right.
11- And the poor.
12- And the wayfarer.
13- And do not squander wastefully.
14- So speak to them a gentle word.
15- And do not make your hand chained.
16- And do not stretch it out to the full.
17- And do not kill your children.
18- And do not approach fornication.
19- And do not kill the soul.
20- So let him not exceed in killing.
21- And fulfil the covenant.
22- And give full measure.
23- And weigh with the right balance.
24- And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge.
25- And do not walk on the earth exultantly.

The indication by "ulāʾika":
The indication in the words of Him the Exalted «كل أولئك كان عنه مسئولا» is to hearing, sight and the heart, and they were indicated by ulāʾika, which is mostly for those with reason because it is the plural of dhā, and dhā is used for those with reason and for those without. Ulāʾ is lengthened for the Hijazis and shortened for the people of Najd and Tamīm, and its more frequent use is for the rational, and its use for the non-rational is rare, like the saying of Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyya:
ذم المنازل بعد منزلة اللوى ... والعيش بعد أولئك الأيام
(Dispraise the dwellings after the dwelling of al-Liwā, and life after those days.)
It is from a poem of his regarded as excellent, whose opening is:
سرت الهموم فبتن غير نيام ... وأخو الهموم يروم كل مرام
(Cares crept on and they spent the night without sleeping, and the man of cares seeks every aim.)
And in it he says after the previous verse:
وإذا وقفت على المنازل باللوى ... فاضت دموعي غير ذات نظام
طرقتك صائدة القلوب وليس ذا ... وقت الزيارة فارجعي بسلام
تجري السواك على أغر كأنه ... برد تحدّر من متون غمام
لو كان عهدك كالذي حدثتنا ... لوصلت ذاك فكان غير رمام
إني أواصل من أردت وصاله ... بحبال لا صلف ولا لوام
(And when I stood at the dwellings at al-Liwā, my tears overflowed, without order. She who hunts hearts visited you by night, and this is not the time for visiting, so go back in peace. She runs the tooth-stick over a bright [mouth] as if it were hail falling from the backs of clouds. Had your pledge been as you told us, I would have joined that and it would not have been worn out. I join the one I wish to join with ropes neither arrogant nor blameworthy.)
And in it, in the satire of al-Farazdaq:
خلق الفرزدق سوءة في مالك ... ولخلف ضبة كان شر غلام
مهلا فرزدق إن قومك فيهم ... خور القلوب وخفّة الأحلام
الظاعنون على العمي بجميعهم ... والنّازلون بشرّ دار مقام
(Al-Farazdaq was created as a disgrace for Mālik, and to Khalaf of Ḍabba he was the worst boy. Gently, Farazdaq! In your people are weakness of hearts and lightness of minds, those who set out in blindness all together, and those who settle in the worst abode.)
Al-Liwā, with kasra on the lām and fatḥa on the wāw, shortened, is originally the end of the sand; it occurs at the beginning of the muʿallaqa of Imruʾ al-Qays, which is:
قفا نبك من ذكرى حبيب ومنزل ... بسقط اللّوى بين الدخول فحومل
(Stop, let us weep, at the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling at the edge of the dune between al-Dakhūl and Ḥawmal.)
It is also a specific place. Yāqūt said: "Poets have mentioned it frequently and confused that Liwā with the sand, so it is hard to separate them; and it is a valley of the valleys of Banū Sulaym."

dervis-irab:73-77.t:
* I'rab:
(وَإِنْ كادُوا لَيَفْتِنُونَكَ عَنِ الَّذِي أَوْحَيْنا إِلَيْكَ لِتَفْتَرِيَ عَلَيْنا غَيْرَهُ) The wāw is resumptive, and إن is the lightened form of the heavy one, and is inoperative; it is also permissible, though rare, for it to operate, as has preceded. كادوا: incomplete past verb, among the verbs of approximation, and the wāw is its noun. The lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa), and the clause يفتنونك is the khabar of كادوا. عن الذي: attached to يفتنونك, which has been made to contain the sense of "turn you away", and for that reason it was made transitive with عن. The clause أوحينا is a ṣila, and إليك is attached to أوحينا. لتفتري: the lām is the lām of reason, and تفتري is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām of reason; علينا: attached to تفتري; the agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; and غيره is the direct object. (وَإِذاً لَاتَّخَذُوكَ خَلِيلًا) The wāw is a conjunction, and إذن is a particle of response (jazāʾ); its answer is implied with the conditional لو, i.e. "and if you had followed their wish and carried out their proposals, for the fulfilment of which they tried to bring you down". The lām prepares for the oath, the implied form being "by Allah, they would have taken you". The kāf is the first direct object and خليلا the second direct object. (وَلَوْلا أَنْ ثَبَّتْناكَ لَقَدْ كِدْتَ تَرْكَنُ إِلَيْهِمْ شَيْئاً قَلِيلًا) لولا is a particle of prevention because of existence. أن and what is in its scope is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, i.e. "had it not been for Our making you firm and Our protecting you". The lām is the answer to لولا, and قد is a particle of affirmation. كاد and its noun; the clause تركن is its khabar; إليهم is attached to تركن; and شيئا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, with the sense of leaning (rukūn), i.e. "a little of leaning". (إِذاً لَأَذَقْناكَ ضِعْفَ الْحَياةِ وَضِعْفَ الْمَماتِ ثُمَّ لا تَجِدُ لَكَ عَلَيْنا نَصِيراً) إذن is a particle of answer and response, its answer also implied with the conditional لو, i.e. "and if you had followed their wish and carried out their proposals, for the fulfilment of which they tried to bring you down". The lām prepares for the oath. أذقناك: verb, agent and direct object. ضعف is a second object, and الحياة is the muḍāf ilayhi; an omitted element must be posited, i.e. "double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death". ثم is a conjunction of delay, and لا is negative. تجد: imperfect verb, its agent latent, its implied form being "you". لك: attached to تجد; علينا: attached to نصيرا; and نصيرا is the direct object. (وَإِنْ كادُوا لَيَسْتَفِزُّونَكَ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ لِيُخْرِجُوكَ مِنْها) The wāw is a conjunction; إن is the lightened form, and it is permissible to make it inoperative or operative. كادوا is among the verbs of approximation, and the wāw is its noun. The lām is the distinguishing lām, and the clause يستفزونك is the khabar of كادوا. من الأرض: attached to يستفزونك; وليخرجوك: attached to يستفزونك; and منها is attached to يخرجوك. The pronoun returns to the land, which is the land of al-Madīna.
(وَإِذاً لا يَلْبَثُونَ خِلافَكَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا) The wāw is a conjunction, and إذن is a particle of response and consequence that is inoperative. لا is negative. يلبثون: imperfect verb, nominative. خلافك, i.e. خلفك ("behind you"), is an adverbial attached to يلبثون, and on it is the saying of the poet:
عفت الديار خلافهم فكأنما ... بسط الشواطب بينهن حصيرا
(The abodes became effaced behind them, as though the strip-splitters had spread a mat among them.)
The poet describes their abodes after them as being effaced and heaped with refuse for lack of sweeping and of anyone to tend them. Al-shawāṭib are the women who split the shaṭb of the date palm, i.e. its green fronds, making them into a mat. إلا is a particle of restriction. قليلا is an adjective of an omitted adverbial, i.e. "a little time", or an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "a brief stay"; so it is an adverbial or a mafʿūl muṭlaq. (سُنَّةَ مَنْ قَدْ أَرْسَلْنا قَبْلَكَ مِنْ رُسُلِنا وَلا تَجِدُ لِسُنَّتِنا تَحْوِيلًا) سنة is made accusative as an emphatic maṣdar, i.e. "Allah established that as a custom".
