Al-Farrāʾ preferred that it be accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "like the custom of Allah"; and according to this parsing one should not pause at قليلا. Others preferred that it be made accusative by an omitted verb, i.e. "follow the custom"; there is no objection to that, as all the views are equal.

* Rhetoric:
- The story of Thaqīf and its proposals:
In these verses are various kinds of rhetoric, and to establish them it is necessary to relate the story of their revelation. It is related that Thaqīf said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We will not enter into your cause until you give us qualities in which we can take pride over the Arabs: that we not be tithed, that we not be mustered, that we not bow (nujabbā) in our prayer, that every usury owed to us be ours and every usury owed by us be waived for us, that you let us enjoy al-Lāt for a year until we take what is offered to it, and when we have taken it we shall break it and become Muslim, and that you declare our valley sacred as you declared Makka sacred; and if the Arabs say 'Why did you do this?', then say 'Allah commanded me to.'" They came with their document and he wrote: "In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. This is a document from Muḥammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Thaqīf: they are not to be tithed and not to be mustered." They said: "And not to bow." The Messenger of Allah was silent. Then they said to the scribe: "Write: and not to bow", while the scribe was looking at the Messenger of Allah. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb stood up, drew his sword and said: "You have kindled the heart of our Prophet, O company of Thaqīf; may Allah kindle your hearts with fire!" They said: "It is not you we are speaking to; we are speaking to Muḥammad." Then it was revealed. Some of the vocabulary must be explained. Their words لا نعشر (in the passive) mean that a tenth of our wealth is not taken from us; ولا نحشر (also passive) means that we are not driven to fight; ولا نجبّى في صلاتنا (also passive), from al-tajbiya, which is, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, that a person stands in the posture of one bowing; Abū ʿUbayda said it occurs in two states, one of which is that he places his hands on his knees, and the other that he falls on his face kneeling, which is prostration. What is meant is "we do not bow and do not prostrate". The story is curious and illustrates important matters.
A- The persistence of the people, their insolence and their persistence in arrogance and haughtiness.
B- The forbearance of the Prophet ﷺ and his taking the people with gentleness and winning-over, in which is the utmost of tact and statecraft.
C- The firmness of ʿUmar and his boldness, and not without reason was he named al-Fārūq. As for the aspects of rhetoric in the verse, they are:
1- Elaboration (iṭnāb) in mentioning this episode, which establishes for you the shrewdness and resourcefulness of the statesman, who takes his people with gentleness and patience and does not let his soul be dissipated in grief while he sees persistence in error and insistence on folly.
2- Exaggeration in minimizing the approach (kaydūda), because the mere gentleness that statecraft requires and the winning-over of the people were held against the Prophet, since a fault grows great according to its doer, in accordance with what is reported, that the good deeds of the righteous are the evil deeds of those brought near.
3- The implicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya) in أذقناك ضعف الحياة; parallels to it have often preceded.
4- Omission: the punishment was omitted out of honour for the station of the Prophet ﷺ. In origin it is a described noun, i.e. "a double punishment in life and a double punishment in death"; then the described noun was omitted and the attribute, namely "double", put in its place, and then the attribute was annexed as the described noun is annexed, so it was said "the double of life and the double of death", as if it were said "We would have made you taste the pain of life and the pain of death".
- Ibn Hishām has an enjoyable section on كاد, which he gave in the sixth chapter of his book al-Mughnī, in warning against matters that became well known among the parsers while the correct view is the opposite:
«Eighteenth: their saying that for كاد, its affirmative is a negation and its negative an affirmation. So when it is said «كاد يفعل» its meaning is that he did not do it, and when it is said «لم يكد يفعل» its meaning is that he did it. The proof of the first is «وإن كادوا ليفتنونك عن الذي أوحينا إليك» and his saying:
«كادت النفس أن تفيض عليه»
(The soul all but flowed out over him.)
and the proof of the second is «وما كادوا يفعلون».
This became so well known among them that al-Maʿarrī made it a riddle, saying:
أنحويّ هذا العصر ما هي لفظة ... جرت في لسائي جرهم وثمود
[Translator's note: the printed text reads «لسائي»; the sense requires «لساني» ("my tongue"), and the second hemistich «لسان جرهم» is probably what is meant.]
إذا استعملت في صورة الجحد أثبتت ... وإن أثبتت قامت مقام جحود
(O grammarian of this age, what is the word that ran on the tongues of Jurhum and Thamūd? When used in the form of denial it affirms, and when affirmed it stands in the place of denial.)
The correct view is that its ruling is the ruling of all other verbs, in that its negation is a negation and its affirmation an affirmation. The explanation is that its meaning is approximation, and there is no doubt that the meaning of «كاد يفعل» is "he came near to doing", and that the meaning of «ما كاد يفعل» is "he did not come near to doing"; so its predicate is always negated. As for when it is negated, it is clear, because if approximation to the act is negated, then the occurrence of that act is negated by reason. Its proof is «إذا أخرج يده لم يكد يراها», and for this reason it is more eloquent than saying «لم يرها», because one who has not seen may have come near to seeing. As for when the approximation is affirmed, it is because informing of the nearness of a thing by custom implies its non-occurrence; otherwise the information would be of its occurrence and not of the approach to its occurrence, since it is not good in custom to say of one who has prayed "he approached prayer", even if he did not pray until he approached prayer. There is no difference in what we have mentioned between كاد and يكاد. If «وما كادوا يفعلون» is raised against this, though they did do it, since what is meant by the act is the slaughter and the Exalted said «فذبحوها», the answer is that it is information about their state at the beginning of the matter, for they were at first far from slaughtering it, by the evidence of what is recited to us of their obstinacy and their repeated questions. Since the like of this became frequent for one from whom approximation to the act was first negated and who then did it afterwards, someone imagined that this very verb is what indicates the occurrence of that very act. It is not so: the occurrence of the act is understood from other evidence, as it was understood in the verse from His words, the Exalted, «فذبحوها».»

dervis-irab:78-81.t:
* Vocabulary:
(لِدُلُوكِ الشَّمْسِ): That is, from the time of its decline. One says dalakat al-shams meaning it set, and it is also said, it declined. Its derivation is from al-dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eyes when looking at it. If dulūk means declining, then the verse includes the five obligatory prayers; and if it means setting, then the noon and afternoon prayers are excluded from it. The origin of this root, that is, whatever has dāl and lām as its first and second radicals, indicates change and movement from one place to another. Thus al-dalba is the singular of al-dalb, a tree with large leaves, no flowers and no fruit, which rises upward in the air as if it had moved from below to above; and from this their saying: «هو من أهل الدّربة، بمعالجة الدّلبة» ("he is one of the people of skill, by working the plane tree"), and from it are made the clappers (nawāqīs), that is, he is a Christian. He watered his land with the dūlāb (water-wheel), with fatḥa on the dāl, and they water with water-wheels, used to carry water from one place to another to irrigate the land. Dalaja comes from al-dalja, which is night travel and moving by night from one place to another; and from it is dalaja and "his eyes streamed", and "how is a western dālij", meaning one who goes back and forth with the bucket from the well to the trough; and "he spent his night dalluj". The poet said:
كأنها وقد براها الإخماس ... ودلج الليل وهاد قياس
شرائح النبع براها القوّاس
(As if she, after the five-day thirst-stages and the night travel had worn her thin, were slivers of nabʿ wood, which the bow-maker pared down.)
Dalaḥa, with the unpointed ḥāʾ, means he walked heavily; dildala aʿḍāʾahu dildalatan means he moved his limbs in walking; and tadaldala fī mashyihi means he shook and swayed in his walking. Dalasa l-ẓalām, "the darkness", is well known, and "he went out in the dalas and ghalas (the darkness before dawn)"; dallasa l-muḥaddith fī ḥadīthihi means the hadith transmitter brought in it something other than the real thing, as if he moved from one event to another, and from this comes the tadlīs of the seller who hides the faults in what he sells and shows its good points. "A land the floods have dalaṣathā" means they moved it from one state to another and made it smooth, and from this comes dirʿ dilāṣ (a smooth, glossy coat of mail). Abū l-Ṭayyib said:
لأمة فاضة أضاة دلاص ... أحكمت نسجها يدا داوود
(A coat of mail, flowing, a pool of glossy sheen, whose weaving the hand of David made firm.)
Dalaʿa and adlaʿa lisānahu means he put his tongue out of his mouth; dalaʿa bi-nafsihi and indalaʿa means he came out and went slack from distress or thirst, as the dog lolls its tongue. Figuratively: indalaʿa l-sayf min ghimdihi wa-indalaqa (the sword sprang from its scabbard), and indalaʿat alsinat al-nīrān (the tongues of flame leapt out). Al-mudallaʿ is one raised in luxury and ease, and the noun is al-dalāʿa; it is a colloquial expression, hence an eloquent colloquialism. Dalafa means he walked like one in fetters; one says "the old man and the fettered man dalafa, dalīfan and dulūfan", which is faster than creeping; shaykh dālif and ʿajāʾiz dawālif. Ṭarafa said:
لا كبير دالف من هرم ... أرهب الناس ولا كلّ الظفر
(Not a creeping, decrepit old man who frightens people, nor one whose claw is blunt.)
And "he came creeping with his load" because of its heaviness. Dalaqa ʿalayhim al-sayl means the flood poured upon them; dalaqat ʿalayhim al-khayl and indalaqat; dalaqū ʿalayhim al-gharra means they launched the raid on them; dalaqa l-baʿīr shiqshiqatahu means the camel brought out its throat-pouch; and "he struck him and his belly's intestines spilled out". Dalaka l-shayʾ means he rubbed it with his hand, which has already been mentioned. Dallahu ʿalā l-ṭarīq means he guided him on the road, and he is the dalīl of the desert. Dallat tadillu, and she is "of beautiful coquetry", that is, she displayed all the charms of her body to captivate others. Dalliha fulān dalhan means he was bewildered and lost his mind from worry or love, so there is in it a figurative movement. Adlaytu dalwī fī l-biʾr means I lowered my bucket into the well; dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr means he dangled his legs from the bed; tadallat al-thamara min al-shajara means the fruit hung from the tree, ready to move from it; adlā bi-ḥaqqihi wa-bi-ḥujjatihi means he presented it, as if moving it to the place of debate. It would take us long to speak if we were to pursue what is in this wonderful root.
(غَسَقِ اللَّيْلِ): Al-ghasaq is darkness. It is also said to be the entering of the first part of the night, as al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said; and it is also said to be the blackness of night and its darkness. Its origin is from flowing: one says ʿasaqat al-ʿayn when its tears flow, as if the darkness poured down upon the world and flowed over them. In al-Asās: "They say 'from the ghasaq to the falaq', which is the entering of the first of the night when the darkness mixes; ghasaqa l-layl yaghsiqu ghasaqan; and Banū Tamīm say aghsaqa." Ibn Qays said:
إن هذا الليل قد غسقا ... واشتكيت الهمّ والأزقا
(This night has grown dark, and I complain of worry and of straits.)
And Jassās said:
أزور إذا ما أغسق الليل خلّتي ... حذار العدى أو أن يرجّم قائل
(I visit my beloved when night darkens, for fear of enemies or lest some speaker cast aspersions.)
(فَتَهَجَّدْ): Al-hujūd is leaving sleep for prayer, and there is disagreement among the lexicographers about it. It is said that it means sleep; it is also said that hujūd is shared between the sleeper and the one who prays. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: "tahajjada: he prayed at night, and tahajjada: he slept", and this is the view of Abū ʿUbayd and al-Layth. The pattern tafaʿʿala comes for removal, as in taḥarraja, taʾaththama and taḥawwaba. In al-Asās: "Hajada l-rajul hujūdan wa-tahajjada: he left sleep for prayer (فَتَهَجَّدْ بِهِ); and bāta fulān mutahajjidan: alone. Hajjadnā: we let him sleep." Labīd said:
قال هجّدنا فقد طال السّرى ... وقدرنا إن خنى الدهر غفل
(He said, "Let us sleep, for the night journey has been long, and we have power [over time], if time's treachery is heedless.")
And in al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj: "Al-hujūd is sleeping by day, al-hujūʿ is sleeping by night, and al-tahajjud is night prayer."
(نافِلَةً): Redundant.

* I'rab:
(أَقِمِ الصَّلاةَ لِدُلُوكِ الشَّمْسِ إِلى غَسَقِ اللَّيْلِ) (أقم الصلاة) is an imperative verb, a latent agent whose implied form is "you", and a direct object. As to the lām in (لدلوك), there are two views. One is that it means "after", that is, after the declining of the sun, like their saying "I wrote my letter for three nights remaining" [Translator's note: «كتبت كتابي لثلاث خلون»], and the meanings of the lām will come in the section on Benefits. The second is that it is in its basic sense, that is, "on account of its declining"; yet the unity of time and the unity of the agent are both absent in «أقم الصلاة لدلوك الشمس»: the agent of standing is the addressee, while the agent of declining is the sun, and their times differ, since the time of performing the prayer comes after the time of declining. For that reason it is put in the genitive with the lām of cause. It is also said that it is for the beginning of the range, and that in the speech a muḍāf is omitted. In every case the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (أقم). As to (إلى غسق الليل), there are two views: one is that it is also attached to (أقم), as the limit of performing the prayer; the second is that it is attached to an omitted ḥāl from (الصلاة), that is "perform it extending to the darkness of the night".
(وَقُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ إِنَّ قُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ كانَ مَشْهُوداً) The wāw is a conjunction. (قرآن) is conjoined to (الصلاة), or is accusative as an incitement (al-ighrāʾ). The first means "and perform the dawn prayer", the prayer being expressed by recitation, which is one of its pillars; the second means "and upon you is the recitation of dawn", that is, hold to it. The first is less strained, and further, the omission of verbal nouns, which are operative, has not been heard of. The clause (إن قرآن …) is a reason for the command; (إن) and its name, and the clause (كان مشهودا) is its khabar; (مشهودا) is the khabar of (كان) and its name is latent, its implied form being "it".
(وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَتَهَجَّدْ بِهِ نافِلَةً لَكَ) The wāw is a conjunction; (من الليل) is attached to (تهجد), that is, "keep vigil with the Qur'an for part of the night". You may also attach it to an omitted verb, that is "stand a standing at night". Al-Ḥawfī said: (من) is attached to a verb indicated by the meaning of the speech, its implied form being "and stay awake part of the night with the Qur'an". The fāʾ is a conjunction; (تهجد) is an imperative verb, its agent latent, its implied form being "you"; (به) is attached to (تهجد); (نافلة) is a ḥāl; and (لك) is an adjective of (نافلة), that is: pray, the prayer being supererogatory for you. It is also permissible for (نافلة) to be a maṣdar like al-ʿāfiya and al-ʿāqiba, in which case it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, the meaning being "perform a supererogatory act". I do not know how some parsed it as an object of (تهجد), when it is an intransitive verb, unless it is said that he embedded in it the meaning of "worship", and how little we need that.
(عَسى أَنْ يَبْعَثَكَ رَبُّكَ مَقاماً مَحْمُوداً) (عسى) is among the verbs of hope, and hope on Allah's part is certain to be fulfilled. The name of (عسى) is latent, and (أن يبعثك) is its khabar. (ربك) is the agent of (يبعثك), or the matter is one of tanāzuʿ (competing governors). (مقاما) is accusative as an adverbial, that is "in a station", or a mafʿūl muṭlaq, because (يبعثك) here means "He will establish you", or a ḥāl, that is "possessing a station". (محمودا) is an adjective of (مقاما).
(وَقُلْ رَبِّ أَدْخِلْنِي مُدْخَلَ صِدْقٍ وَأَخْرِجْنِي مُخْرَجَ صِدْقٍ) (رب) is a vocative from which the vocative particle has been omitted. (أدخلني) is a verb of supplication, a latent agent, and the yāʾ is a direct object. (مدخل صدق) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq because it is a maṣdar mīmī, and its annexation to (صدق) is the annexation of the described to its description, or is for clarification. (وأخرجني مخرج صدق) is conjoined to the corresponding clause.
(وَاجْعَلْ لِي مِنْ لَدُنْكَ سُلْطاناً نَصِيراً) (واجعل) is conjoined to (أدخلني) and (أخرجني). (لي) is the second object of (اجعل) and (سلطانا) is the first object of (اجعل). (نصيرا) is an adjective. (ومن لدنك) is a ḥāl, because it was an adjective of (سلطانا), or it is attached to whatever the first is attached to.
(وَقُلْ جاءَ الْحَقُّ وَزَهَقَ الْباطِلُ) That is: say when you enter Mecca as a conqueror. The clause (جاء الحق) is the content of the saying, and (زهق الباطل) is conjoined to it.
(إِنَّ الْباطِلَ كانَ زَهُوقاً) (إن) and its name, and the clause (كان) is its khabar, and (زهوقا) is the khabar of (كان).

* Rhetoric:
In His saying «وقل جاء الحق وزهق الباطل ان الباطل كان زهوقا»:
The art of the appended clause (al-tadhyīl), which is when the poet or prose writer appends to his speech, after it is complete and silence upon it is fitting, a sentence that confirms what precedes and increases its emphasis, and which runs in the manner of a proverb to add confirmation. The difference between it and takmīl (completion) is that takmīl comes to a meaning that needs perfecting, while tadhyīl adds nothing except confirmation and emphasis of the first statement. This verse is among the greatest proofs of it, since the last sentence is the appended clause that came out in the manner of a circulating proverb. Among its poetic examples is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:
ولست بمستبق أخا لا تلمّه ... على شعث أيّ الرجال المهذّب
(You will not retain a brother whom you do not set right in his disarray; which man is refined?)
That is, the one whose deeds are free of fault and whose qualities are pleasing. The first part of the verse indicates by its implication the negation of the perfect among men, and its second part is a confirmation and affirmation of that, since the question in it is one of denial, that is, there is no refined man among men. The scholars of badīʿ agreed that his saying «أي الرجال المهذب» is one of the best tadhyīl in poetry, because it came out as a proverb, and hence they said that al-Nābigha was the best poet of people by a quarter of a verse.

* Benefits:
1- The glad tidings were fulfilled, the command of Allah came, and Muḥammad entered Mecca as a conqueror, as is well known in the history of the Sīra. Jibrīl said to Muḥammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he came down with this verse on the day of the conquest: "Take your staff, then throw it." So he went to the idols one by one, prodding each in the eye with the staff and saying, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished", and the idol fell on its face, until he had thrown them all down. There remained the idol of Khuzāʿa on top of the Kaʿba, made of yellow glass. He said, "ʿAlī, throw it down." So he climbed up, threw it and smashed it, to the end of this unique story.
2- The meanings of the prepositional lām:
Ibn Hishām in Mughnī l-Labīb gave twenty-two meanings for the prepositional lām, whereas others were content to mention only twelve and denied that it has these other meanings. The following is a useful summary of that: 1- Ownership, as in «لله ما في السموات».
2- Quasi-ownership. Ibn Hishām made this class two: specification, as in al-sarj lil-dābba ("the saddle is for the mount"), and entitlement, which occurs between a meaning and a person, as in «العزة لله» and "the command is Allah's".
3- Transitivisation to the direct object, as in «فهب لي من لدنك وليا». Ibn Hishām and others preferred to exemplify it with "mā aḍraba Zaydan li-ʿAmr" ("how much Zayd beats ʿAmr!"), because ḍaraba is originally transitive, but when the verb of wonder is built from it, it is moved to the pattern fuʿula with ḍamma on the ʿayn and becomes intransitive; it is then made transitive by the hamza to Zayd and by the lām to ʿAmr.
4- Cause, as in the saying of Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī:
وإني لتعروني لذكراك هزة ... كما انتفض العصفور بلّله القطر
(A tremor comes over me at remembering you, as the sparrow shakes when the rain has wetted it.)
That is, on account of my remembering you.
5- Emphasis, which is the redundant lām, and it has kinds, among them:
a- The lām interposed between a transitive verb and its object, as in the saying of Ibn Mayyāda al-Rammāḥ praising ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān:
وملكت ما بين العراق ويثرب ... ملكا أجار لمسلم ومعاهد
(You ruled what lies between Iraq and Yathrib, a rule that gave protection to a Muslim and a covenanted person.)
That is, it protected a Muslim and a covenanted person.
b- Among them is the lām thrust in between the two terms of a genitive construct, as in the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā:
سئمت تكاليف الحياة ومن يعش ... ثمانين حولا لا أبا لك يسأم
(I am weary of life's burdens, and whoever lives eighty years, lā abā laka, grows weary.)
The original is «lā abāka mawjūd» ("your father is not to be found"), an expression that can carry praise or blame, and what follows it is put in the genitive by annexation.
c- Among them is the lām of calling for help (lām al-mustaghāth), which is redundant according to the verifiers, by the evidence that dropping it is sound.
6- Strengthening an operator that has become weak, either by being derivative in operation, like the maṣdar, the active and passive participles and the forms of intensity, as in «مصدقا لما معهم» and «فعّال لما يريد», or by being postponed after its object, as in «إن كنتم للرؤيا تعبرون», the original being «إن كنتم تعبرون الرؤيا»; when the verb was postponed and its object put before it, its operation became weak and was strengthened by the lām. Ibn Hishām in al-Mughnī made it redundant, but the sounder view is that it is not.
7- Agreement with (إلى), that is, for the end of a range, as in «كل يجري لأجل مسمى», that is, «إلى أجل مسمى».
8- The oath, which is specific to the Name of Majesty because it is a substitute for the tāʾ, as in: lillāhi lā yuʾakhkharu l-ajal ("by Allah, the appointed term is not delayed").
9- Wonder, as in lillāhi darruk, meaning "how abundant is your gift!" It is most often used in the vocative, as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
فيا لك من ليل كأن نجومه ... بكل مغار الفتل شدت بيذبل
(O what a night! It is as if its stars were fastened to Yadhbul with every tightly twisted rope.)
10- Result, consequence or outcome, as in «فالتقطه آل فرعون ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا» and the saying of Abū l-ʿAtāhiya:
لدوا للموت وابنوا للخراب
(Bear children for death and build for ruin.)
For death is not the reason for bearing children, nor is ruin the reason for building, but their consequence and outcome became that. Al-Zamakhsharī denied it and said: "The verified view is that it is the lām of cause, and that the causality in it is figurative, not literal."
11- Posteriority, as in «أقم الصلاة لدلوك الشمس», already mentioned, because the time enters, and we know it, by the declining, so the prayer is not performed except after the declining, which is the sun's inclination from its zenith. From it also is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: «صوموا لرؤيته وأفطروا لرؤيته» ("Fast at its sighting and break the fast at its sighting"), and the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:
فلما تفرقنا كأني ومالكا ... لطول اجتماع لم نبت ليلة معا
(When we parted, it was as if Mālik and I, despite long companionship, had never spent a night together.)
12- Superiority, that is, agreement with (على) in the literal sense, as in «يخرون للأذقان», plural of dhaqn, meaning upon them; and figuratively, as in «وإن أسأتم فلها», that is, «فعليها».
13- Agreement with (في), as in «قل إنما علمها عند ربي لا يجليها لوقتها إلا هو», that is, "none discloses it in its time except Him".
14- Agreement with (عند), as in the reading of al-Ḥajūrī «بل كذبوا بالحق لما جاءهم» with kasra on the lām and lightening of the lām, that is, "at its coming to them".
15- Agreement with (مع), as in the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra mentioned above: «فلما تفرقنا …» etc.
16- Agreement with (من), as in "I heard a cry from him" [«سمعت له صراخا»], and the saying of Jarīr:
لنا الفضل في الدنيا وأنفك راغم ... ونحن لكم يوم القيامة أفضل
(Ours is the excellence in this world, though your nose be in the dust, and on the Day of Resurrection we are better than you.)
That is, «ونحن منكم أفضل».
17- Conveying, as in «قل لعبادي», and its rule is that it governs the noun of the hearer of a saying.
18- Agreement with (عن) when used with speaking, as in «وقال الذين كفروا للذين آمنوا لو كان خيرا ما سبقونا إليه».
19- Bestowal of possession, as in: "I gave Zayd a dinar."
20- Cause, as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
ويوم عقرت للعذارى مطيتي ... فيا عجبا من كورها المتحمل
(And on the day I hamstrung my mount for the maidens, O what a wonder, its saddle borne and carried!)
Among them is the lām that enters in form upon the imperfect, as in «وأنزلنا إليك الذكر لتبين للناس», and the verb after it is put in the accusative by an implied (أن).
21- Emphasis of negation, which is the lām that enters in form upon a verb preceded by (ما كان) or (لم يكن), as in «وما كان الله ليطلعكم على الغيب». Most grammarians call it the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd).
22- Clarification, already mentioned, which we repeat here in detail. It is of three kinds:
a- The one that distinguishes the object from the agent. Its rule is that it occurs after a verb of wonder or an elative that convey love or hatred; you say "mā aḥabbanī" and "mā abghaḍanī". If you say «li-fulān» ("to so-and-so"), you are the agent of love and hatred and he is their object; if you say «ilā fulān», the matter is the reverse.
b and c- The one that makes clear an agency not confused with objecthood, and the one that makes clear an objecthood not confused with agency, where what accompanies each is either not known from what came before it, or is known but its clarification is resumed to strengthen and emphasise the clarification. In all this the lām is attached to an omitted element. An example of the one clarifying objecthood: saqyan li-Zayd and jadʿan lahu ("may Zayd be given to drink", "may he be maimed"). This lām is not attached to the maṣdar nor to their implied verbs, because both are transitive, nor does it strengthen an operator weak by derivation; it is a lām that clarifies the one for whom or against whom the invocation is made.
There was disagreement over His saying, the Exalted, «هيهات هيهات لما توعدون». It is said that the lām is redundant and (ما) is the agent; it is also said that the agent is a latent pronoun referring to the resurrection and the bringing forth, so that the lām is for clarification. The discussion of the lām is long, and it is referred to the longer works.
